entries.title: Train Qwen3 on AWS Trainium with torchtitan
entries.summary: Train Qwen3 on AWS Trainium with torchtitan three ways on a single trn2.48xlarge: the Hugging Face Transformers v5 modeling backend, torchtitan's native Qwen3, and NKI mixture-of-experts kernels. The same torchrun launcher and config structure work unchanged across all three paths, including loading and saving published Hugging Face safetensors.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Train Qwen3 on AWS Trainium with torchtitan

Using torchtitan on AWS Trainium means using it the way you always have. TorchNeuron registers Trainium as a native PyTorch device, which lets torchtitan use it through standard PyTorch interfaces. You can use these configurations to pre-train from random initialization or fine-tune published weights. You can also customize the model implementation and kernels for your workload. In this post, you train Qwen3 three ways on a single 

trn2.48xlarge
.

The first method uses Transformers v5 as a modeling backend in torchtitan. It runs Hub models through 

AutoModelForCausalLM
and reads and writes published safetensors directly. The second method switches to torchtitan’s native Qwen3 by changing 
config.model_spec
. The third adds Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) mixture-of-experts (MoE) kernels from the torchtitan-neuron recipes and then uses torchtitan’s override registry to attach your own kernel. All three configurations use the same 
torchrun
launch pattern and config structure.

Prerequisites

To follow this walkthrough, use a single 

trn2.48xlarge
with either the AWS Deep Learning AMI for Neuron or a Neuron PyTorch training container. Both environments provide the Neuron driver, runtime, and compiler required to train on Trainium.

Before you install torchtitan-neuron, check whether your environment already includes it. The following command prints the installed version and package path:

This walkthrough uses the versions in the following table. To reproduce the examples, pin these versions. The Transformers v5 integration and Trainium-specific override modules can change between torchtitan releases.

ComponentVersion
Instancetrn2.48xlarge, 16 Trainium2 accelerators, 128 physical NeuronCores
Logical NeuronCores64 at LNC=2
torch, torch_neuronx2.14.0, 2.14.3
transformers5.16.0
torchtitan-neuronrelease-2.33 (0.2.2+neuron.1)

When 

torch_neuronx
is installed, TorchNeuron registers Trainium as the 
neuron
device and torchtitan detects it at startup. In eager mode, Neuron compiles operations as they execute. With 
torch.compile
, Neuron compiles the captured graph. This same launch pattern works across all three configurations.

For the versions used in this walkthrough, install torchtitan-neuron and torchtitan’s remaining dependencies with 

--no-deps
to preserve the Neuron build of torch:

Before you start training, get the Qwen3 model artifacts from Hugging Face Hub. Store them in a local directory that you can pass to the training config:

Each training configuration is a Python config function. The three examples start from a base config that you update for each step.

Train with Hugging Face Transformers v5

In the first configuration, Transformers v5 builds Qwen3 through 

AutoModelForCausalLM
. The Hub model definition supplies the implementation used for the forward and backward passes. You select the model by setting its Hub ID in the config.

Start with 

transformers_modeling_backend_full()
. It leaves the fields that map to Hugging Face configuration keys unset, so 
AutoConfig.from_pretrained()
loads the model architecture from the Hub.

Create 

neuron_qwen3.py
in the torchtitan-neuron repository root, where you run the training command. Add the imports, model artifact path, and base config:

This command launches 64 training processes, one for each logical NeuronCore. 

--module neuron_qwen3
imports the local config module. 
--config v5_qwen3_4b
selects the configuration function. The data parallel setting shards the model across all 64 ranks.

Load and save Hugging Face checkpoints

To fine-tune from published weights, enable checkpoint loading and point 

initial_load_path
to 
ASSETS
. The state-dictionary adapter adjusts the leading 
model.
prefix and handles tied embeddings. It saves the final checkpoint as Hugging Face safetensors.

Use the first training-step loss as a quick check that torchtitan loaded the published weights. For 

Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507
, the verified run produced a step 1 loss of 6.54 from published weights and 12.43 from random initialization.

After training, load the exported checkpoint with 

AutoModelForCausalLM
and 
load_state_dict
. A successful round trip reports no missing or unexpected keys other than 
lm_head.weight
, which Qwen3-4B ties to the token embeddings. This confirms that the files remain a standard Hugging Face checkpoint.

Train with torchtitan’s native models

In the second configuration, torchtitan builds its native 

Qwen3Model
. Add the native Qwen3 imports and config function to 
neuron_qwen3.py
:

This example starts from 

qwen3_32b()
because the tested torchtitan build does not provide a generic 
qwen3_4b()
config builder. The next line replaces the 32B model specification with the 4B specification. The remaining fields reproduce the tested run.

config.model_spec
selects the model class and defines how torchtitan shards the model and maps its checkpoint keys. Here, 
model_registry("4B", attn_backend="sdpa")
selects torchtitan’s native Qwen3 implementation with scaled dot product attention (SDPA).

Add NKI kernels for mixture of experts

In the third configuration, torchtitan runs mixture-of-experts layers with kernels written in NKI, the Neuron kernel language. Add the required imports and Qwen3 MoE config function to 

neuron_qwen3.py
:

This configuration uses data parallel sharding across 64 ranks with a tensor parallel degree of 1. It does not use expert parallelism. 

num_experts=64
sets the number of experts in the model, not the expert parallel degree.

Setting 

CompileConfig(enable=False)
runs this example in eager mode. TorchNeuron supports registered NKI operators in both eager execution and 
torch.compile
.

In the torchtitan build used for this walkthrough, 

qwen3_nki_moe_config()
replaces the MoE block with the NKI grouped-experts implementation. It also selects SDPA and the gather-free rotary embedding. When you enable 
torch.compile
, add 
"grad_clip"
to 
CompileConfig.components
to compile gradient-norm clipping.

NKI kernels enter training as PyTorch operators. 

wrap_nki
makes an NKI kernel callable from PyTorch, and 
nki_op
registers the operator. 
register_autograd
attaches its backward pass using routing metadata saved during the forward pass.

The example reduces Qwen3-30B-A3B to 4 layers and 64 experts so it fits on one 

trn2.48xlarge
. It routes each token to 4 experts with 
top_k=4
.

Attach your own NKI kernel

In some cases, you might want to optimize an operation for the tensor shapes in your model. A specialized kernel can tailor its tiling and data movement to those shapes. It can also replace a performance-critical sequence of PyTorch operations with one optimized operator. You can write the kernel yourself or start with one from 

nkilib
. This example uses 
rope_hf
from 
nkilib.core.embeddings
, which expects the Hugging Face tensor layout and supports its own backward mode. This example demonstrates kernel registration and autograd integration, not a performance improvement.

Create 

my_neuron_kernels.py
in the repository root, where you launch training. torchtitan stores query and key as 
[batch, seq, heads, head_dim]
, whereas 
rope_hf
expects 
[batch, heads, seq, head_dim]
. Convert the layout inside the operator and allocate the output tensors with 
torch.empty_like()
:

rope_hf
computes gradients when you call it with 
backward=True
. Register a second operator for that mode. Save the rotary cache during the forward pass so the backward pass can reuse it. Return 
None
for the cache gradient because the cache is not differentiable.

Because 

rope_hf
requires a supported sequence length, validate that constraint before calling the kernel. Subclass 
CosSinRoPE
and call 
rope_fwd
from 
apply_rotary_emb
:

Register 

NKIRoPE
as the replacement for 
CosSinRoPE
. 
derive()
copies the shared configuration fields into the replacement config:

To load the custom override, pass its module name to 

--override.imports
. torchtitan imports the registry entry before it builds the model:

Before training starts, torchtitan logs each config node that the override replaces. Confirm that the output contains one 

nki_rope
entry for each Qwen3 layer:

Set the sequence length to a multiple of 

128 * LNC
, which is 256 when LNC is 2. Reshape the rotary cache to 
[seq, head_dim * 2]
, with cosine values in the first half and sine values in the second. The kernel validates these constraints before training begins.

For a complete torchtitan example, see 

torchtitan_neuron/models/gpt_oss/nki_attention.py
. It connects 
nkilib
flash-attention kernels through the same operator and override mechanisms. It also handles 
DTensor
inputs for tensor parallelism.

Before you train with a custom kernel, compare its outputs with the implementation it replaces. In the numerical test with float32 inputs, 

rope_hf
and torchtitan’s PyTorch rotary embedding produced a maximum absolute difference of 0.0 for both query and key.

When you register multiple overrides, limit each one to the intended module instances with 

fqns
. For example, 
fqns=["layers.1[0-9].attention.rope"]
targets the rotary embedding in layers 10 through 19. torchtitan stops when two overrides claim the same node and warns when an override matches no nodes.

Review the training output

At startup, confirm that torchtitan reports 64 ranks and the expected model. The first step includes compilation and takes longer than later steps. Each training step reports the loss, gradient norm, high-bandwidth memory (HBM) usage, throughput, and model FLOPs utilization (MFU). For the checkpoint run, confirm that the first-step loss is near 6.54. For the custom kernel run, confirm that the 

nki_rope
override appears once for each Qwen3 layer.

Scale across the instance

The same parallelism settings apply to the Transformers and native model configurations. A 

trn2.48xlarge
exposes 64 logical NeuronCores at LNC=2. Set 
data_parallel_shard_degree = -1
to shard the model parameters, gradients, and optimizer state across every rank that 
torchrun
starts.

Set 

config.parallelism.tensor_parallel_degree
to shard each layer’s weights across a group of ranks. Each rank computes a slice of every matrix multiplication. With sequence parallelism enabled by default, normalization layers run on activations sharded along the sequence dimension. torchtitan combines tensor parallelism with Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) on a multidimensional 
DeviceMesh
.

Watch per-rank HBM as you increase the model size, sequence length, or local batch size. These values determine how much memory each rank requires.

Clean up

If you want to keep your checkpoints, copy them to persistent storage before you clean up. If you plan to reuse the instance, stop it. When you no longer need the instance, terminate it.

Conclusion

AWS Trainium works as a supported torchtitan device across all three configurations in this walkthrough. You can train Qwen3 through Hugging Face Transformers v5 and load or save published safetensors directly. You can also train with torchtitan’s native Qwen3 implementation by setting 

config.model_spec
. For mixture-of-experts models, use the torchtitan-neuron NKI recipes. For custom kernels, use the override registry to attach NKI operators through the same launch flow.

For setup guidance, see the AWS Neuron documentation. For current source and training recipes, see the torchtitan repository.

entries.title: How U.S. Hunger connects leaders and data using Amazon Quick
entries.summary: U.S. Hunger, a nonprofit addressing food insecurity, uses Amazon Quick to connect organizational data with leadership decisions. Leaders explore applicant data directly, share KPI definitions and financial context in Quick Spaces, and investigate policy questions with Quick Research.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

How U.S. Hunger connects leaders and data using Amazon Quick

For U.S. Hunger, feeding families takes more than delivering food to them. It takes understanding the people behind each request, the pressures they face, and the business that makes the mission possible. That means connecting information across the organization. Its mission is to feed families today and unite them to a healthier tomorrow.

U.S. Hunger reports delivering more than 250 million meals. Its work has reached 59 countries historically and is now concentrated primarily in the United States. The organization reports approximately 500 percent growth over four years, compared with only 15–20 percent headcount growth. For a lean team at that scale, every hour and every decision matters.

With Amazon Quick, U.S. Hunger can explore organizational data directly, colleagues can work from shared definitions, and leaders can examine financial information alongside the circumstances families report. U.S. Hunger’s experience shows how those capabilities fit into the daily work of a lean nonprofit.

From banking to feeding families

Rick Whitted spent 30 years in banking before making the leap to lead U.S. Hunger. His connection to food insecurity, however, began long before that career change.

When Rick and his wife were in their mid-twenties, he left his career to start a business. They lost everything. Even though he went to work every day, they relied on help from family to get by. He remembers coming home to find a pantry box on the table, left by aunts or grandparents. Seeing that box broke him.

More than 20 years later, when the board chair asked him to consider leading U.S. Hunger, his wife reminded him of those days, when their own family needed help putting food on the table. To her, leading U.S. Hunger was a chance to help families going through what they had experienced themselves. Rick cried, called the chair back, and accepted.

“The families we serve today, their stories are my story.”

— Rick Whitted, President and CEO, U.S. Hunger

More than six years into the role, that personal connection remains at the heart of Rick’s leadership.

From data requests to direct exploration

U.S. Hunger first learned about Quick through an AWS Social Entrepreneur Accelerator event led by Kat Esser. Rick saw an opportunity to explore the organization’s data directly, following questions as they arose without asking the technology team for a new data pull each time.

Chief technology officer (CTO) Ezekiel Brooks helped make that possible by giving Rick access to core datasets from Full Cart, U.S. Hunger’s food-assistance program. Full Cart delivers donor-funded food directly to households in need. Quick gave Rick room to explore the information at his own pace and ask follow-up questions. The organization’s data became his sandbox.

The data comes from Impact Manager, U.S. Hunger’s proprietary cloud-based data platform supporting its food-assistance work. Quick pulls data from SQL Server into its in-memory engine, SPICE, through scheduled refresh jobs at 2 AM ET each night. The technology team and a colleague working with research data prepare the datasets and provide definitions to help Rick interpret the information.

Direct exploration was the starting point, but the moment when everything clicked came with a different discovery: Quick Spaces.

The moment Quick became an enterprise tool

For Rick, Spaces changed the role Quick could play in the organization. A Space gives colleagues a shared place to work with documents, definitions, and analyses relevant to a particular area of the business.

That matters when leaders need to understand one another’s work and make decisions together. Shared definitions of key performance indicators (KPIs) help them agree on what a measure means. Financial documents and planning tools provide context for discussions about the organization’s resources. Rick sees this as his a-ha moment: using Quick to help the leadership team run the organization together.

“Quick provides a live connection to how leadership thinks through problems. I can pick up where our CEO left off in a financial model or see how he’s framing a KPI, without scheduling another meeting.”

— Sarah Aranguibel, Chief of Staff, U.S. Hunger

The leadership team brings together a shared document of KPIs, developed over more than a year while working across NetSuite, Salesforce, Impact Manager, and its payroll system. The document records definitions, where measures come from, and goals. Rick also uses Quick to develop definitions for client tiers and shares them in the same Space.

“With all the knowledge and data we have, Space reduces as much noise as possible and narrows my discussion.”

— Rick Whitted, President and CEO, U.S. Hunger

Selecting the Space relevant to a question keeps the conversation focused on the right documents. The financial Space is shared with the CTO, chief operating officer (COO), and finance leadership, giving colleagues access to the tools and business context behind an analysis.

Together, these materials show colleagues what the organization measures and the business logic behind it.

What Quick does for the team, day to day

U.S. Hunger has given 17 colleagues access to Quick across its executive leadership, technology team, Full Cart program, Finance, Compliance, and supporting functions. For its CEO, chat is the primary day-to-day artificial intelligence (AI) workspace, and Spaces is the capability he uses most.

Improving call reporting

Using a Space containing Salesforce call reports, Rick is drafting instructions for the technology team: which measures to include, where the data comes from, and what each measure means. In Quick, he can comment directly on the generated draft and regenerate it with multiple changes incorporated. He can review and refine the instructions alongside the source reports, without spending time moving documents and comments between Word and chat.

After completion, the instructions will guide reporting improvements for the member-engagement team, helping the program’s operational leaders and COO monitor the team’s work.

Research and policy

U.S. Hunger uses Amazon Quick Research to investigate current events, inform communications, and connect policy questions with its survey data. The CEO is also exploring how that data could serve a wider audience. With the version history in Quick Research, he can revisit earlier versions as he refines an investigation.

Understanding food insecurity requires information about who is struggling and the circumstances behind that struggle. In September 2025, the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) announced that it would end future Household Food Security Reports. With that longstanding reporting series ending, access to other sources of evidence becomes especially important.

U.S. Hunger wants to make the information it collects available beyond its own organization. It envisions a national hunger-data resource where researchers and the public can explore the experiences of families seeking assistance. Alongside that access, the organization plans an enterprise offering that companies can purchase, helping fund its mission.

As Rick puts it, the goal is for “the very data we’re using to help people” to become “the flywheel that feeds the very people we’re trying to help.”

Executive insight and financial planning

The national dashboard brings food insecurity together with income, education, health, and social needs. Filters help leaders examine different populations and use those findings in conversations with prospective partners about why families need help.

For financial planning, Rick uses a Space containing audits, cash-flow information, and board budget views. A debt-service calculator and nonprofit financial-health worksheet help him share his banking experience with the COO. The financial documents provide context for drafting audit footnotes.

With over a decade of financial documents available in the Space, Rick can ask Quick to compare patterns over time and explore questions about current operations. His familiarity with the source material helps him check the answers and challenge conclusions the evidence doesn’t support.

Together, these workflows help Rick use Quick to explore both sides of the organization’s mission: understanding the families who need support and planning the finances that help U.S. Hunger provide it.

Technology as social impact

Putting food in an empty pantry meets an immediate need. Understanding what keeps that pantry empty means looking at the circumstances inside the home and the pressures around it, including income, housing, employment, and health.

U.S. Hunger combines structured survey responses with narrative testimony collected since 2020. Its records include more than 300,000 applicants. Behind those records are lives, lived experiences, and families.

Affordability is a central theme. Among respondents to the questions shown, 90.1 percent say they sometimes or often can’t afford balanced meals. Separately, 97 percent report difficulty paying for basics such as food, housing, medical care, and heating.

“In reality, it’s about affordability.”

— Rick Whitted, President and CEO, U.S. Hunger

The team supplies business definitions alongside the data. U.S. Hunger uses classification codes known as Z codes to categorize reported social and economic circumstances, including food insecurity, low income, and housing difficulties. Together, these views form what Rick calls “an EKG reading on hunger.”

Food insecurity is the most frequently recorded Z code in this view, followed by low income. The other leading categories concern housing or financial circumstances. Leaders can examine the pressures accompanying requests for food, rather than looking at food needs in isolation.

Another view shows 44.7 percent of all applicants reporting illness and 79.1 percent enrolled in health insurance. In the employment view, 64.4 percent say they don’t need or want help finding or keeping work.

These findings show why requests for food assistance need to be understood alongside families’ wider circumstances. Having health insurance doesn’t necessarily remove financial pressure, and help finding work is not what every applicant is seeking.

U.S. Hunger has been working to organize its data to better understand the pressures families face. Quick helps the team visualize patterns in that information. Rick describes one pattern as an early warning signal: periodic difficulty obtaining enough food, before families reach daily or weekly food insecurity.

“We were on that journey, but [Quick] really helped us visualize that and lay that out much faster.”

— Rick Whitted, President and CEO, U.S. Hunger

For Rick, this is where technology becomes a form of social impact. Quick helps U.S. Hunger look past a request for groceries to the pressures behind it. Feeding a family meets today’s need. Understanding those pressures is part of helping that family toward a healthier tomorrow.

A message to other nonprofits

“501C is a tax designation. You’re still a corporation, which means you’re a business. And if you’re a business not embracing technology, you will get left behind – or your mission will cost you more.”

— Rick Whitted, President and CEO, U.S. Hunger

A nonprofit still has a business to run. Its leaders need to understand cash flow, agree on what performance measures mean, and connect operational decisions to their mission. U.S. Hunger uses Quick to bring that work together. Financial documents give Rick context for planning. Shared KPI definitions give colleagues a common reference. Dashboards help leaders examine the circumstances behind requests for food.

Getting started didn’t require every system to be connected. Historical financial documents and questions Rick already needed to answer gave him a practical starting point. Other nonprofits can begin with a question that matters to their work and relevant information they have available.

The people who know the organization remain the subject matter experts. They supply the context, check the answers, and decide what action makes sense. Quick helps them examine the evidence and bring it into those decisions.

“This is not about bringing humans into the AI loop. It’s about bringing AI into the human loop.”

— Rick Whitted, President and CEO, U.S. Hunger

What comes next for U.S. Hunger and Amazon Quick

U.S. Hunger is developing an enterprise KPI framework during Q4 2026. Boomi already connects NetSuite, Salesforce, and Impact Manager. The organization plans to use Boomi to bring research data, historical analytics, and enterprise KPIs into Amazon Redshift, which will supply data to Quick through scheduled SPICE jobs. Figure 6 shows the architecture supporting that planned expansion.

The diagram shows a planned pipeline bringing information from Impact Manager, NetSuite, Salesforce, Paylocity, ThriveLink, and iQpay through Boomi into Amazon Redshift. Scheduled SPICE jobs then supply the data to Quick.

The next step for U.S. Hunger is to explore how its hunger data could become a national resource for researchers, the public, and companies. Rick has asked AWS for help shaping that work. The ambition extends the role of technology beyond internal analysis: Knowledge gathered while helping families could support research and generate revenue to help feed more families.

Conclusion

U.S. Hunger’s goal remains to feed families today and unite them to a healthier tomorrow. Direct data exploration, shared executive context, research, and financial analysis help its leaders understand both the organization they run and the families at the center of its mission.

Watch the video

Hear more from Rick Whitted in episode 8 of the Quick-witted podcast, “From Silos to Solutions.” He discusses how U.S. Hunger uses Amazon Quick and the role technology plays in its mission.

Learn more about U.S. Hunger and explore Amazon Quick capabilities and customer stories.

entries.title: Beyond the KV cache: Training and serving i14’s Laplace 3B linear attention model on AWS Trainium2 with native PyTorch
entries.summary: Learn how i14 trained and served Laplace 3B, a linear attention model, on AWS Trainium2 using native PyTorch. Its recurrent state stays fixed at 29.5 MB per sequence regardless of context length, avoiding the growing key-value cache of transformer models and keeping serving memory predictable.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Beyond the KV cache: Training and serving i14’s Laplace 3B linear attention model on AWS Trainium2 with native PyTorch

Most large language models (LLMs) use transformer architectures with softmax attention. During inference, their key-value (KV) cache grows with the conversation or document context. This can reduce concurrency, increase serving cost, and force agentic applications to discard useful history.

i14 designed Laplace 3B as a linear attention alternative. Its recurrent state stays at 29.5 MB per sequence, independent of context length. Working with AWS, i14 used native PyTorch support through TorchNeuron Native to bring this custom architecture to AWS Trainium2. This preserved its Gated Linear Attention (GLA) design and Muon optimizer.

On one trn2.48xlarge instance, Laplace 3B trained at about 120,000 tokens per second. The model served 11,544 output tokens per second across 1,280 concurrent sequences. This post explains the model design, the changes i14 made for Trainium2, and the training and inference results.

About i14

i14 is an AI research and technology company that develops model architectures, components, and runtimes. Its work draws on AI, computational cognitive science, and research into how biological systems learn over time. i14 applies these ideas to models that can retain long-range context without allowing serving state to grow with every token.

Why linear attention models?

Transformer softmax attention compares tokens across the context. During training, this computation grows quadratically with sequence length. During inference, the KV cache grows as the model processes more tokens.

Linear attention reorganizes the computation around a recurrent state that is updated for each token. Laplace 3B uses GLA to compress prior context into a fixed-size matrix state. This changes training attention from O(T2) to O(T) and keeps inference state fixed at 29.5 MB per sequence.

ConsiderationTransformer softmax attentionLaplace 3B with GLA
Training attentionBuilds pairwise token scores with O(T2) scalingUpdates chunked recurrent state with O(T) scaling
Inference memoryKV cache grows with contextRecurrent state remains fixed in size
Longer contextsEach sequence consumes more accelerator memoryContext length does not increase recurrent-state allocation
ImplementationUses widely optimized attention kernelsRequires architecture-specific kernels and compiler tuning

Linear attention compresses history rather than retaining every key and value. You must therefore evaluate retrieval quality for your workloads. The fixed state can benefit long-running agents, large-document analysis, and applications that need persistent memory with predictable serving requirements.

How i14 adapted Laplace 3B for AWS Trainium2

The original implementation of Laplace 3B used GPU-optimized Triton kernels. The AWS Generative AI Innovation Center (GenAIIC) team first rewrote the GLA kernel with standard PyTorch operators for Trainium2. After comparing both approaches, the team chose the beta version of TorchNeuron Native, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium, because it performed better.

The implementation required three changes:

  • Using native PyTorch for the GLA attention kernel. The team replaced the GPU-specific fused_chunk_simple_gla Triton kernel with standard PyTorch operators, using 16 chunks of 128 tokens to match the 128 partitions of the NeuronCore on-chip buffer.
  • Redesigning how Muon communicates. Two all_to_all collectives in MuonFSDP2 cut per-rank traffic by 24 times and raised throughput by 1.63 times.
  • Compiling the sequential backward pass. The team statically unrolled the 16 chunk steps of the GLA recurrence to fit the graph-size and on-chip memory limits of the compiler.

The engineering challenges section describes each change in detail.

Why AWS Trainium accelerators?

AWS Trainium is a family of AWS machine learning (ML) accelerators designed for model training and inference. A trn2.48xlarge instance combines 16 Trainium2 chips, 64 logical NeuronCores, high-bandwidth memory, and NeuronLink-v3 connectivity. These resources support the distributed training and inference configurations described in this post.

Three properties of Trainium2 shaped the implementation: software-managed on-chip memory (Challenge 1), a fast chip-to-chip interconnect (Challenge 2), and a static compiler (Challenge 3). The compiler traces the GLA recurrence as a fixed graph.

Software-managed on-chip memory. Each NeuronCore has a 28 MiB State Buffer (SBUF) with 128 partitions and a 2 MiB partial-sum buffer (PSUM). The PSUM is wired to a 128×128 systolic Tensor Engine, alongside separate vector and scalar units. The SBUF is not a cache: the compiler schedules every 

HBM-to-SBUF
transfer ahead of time, so the data is in place with no evictions or misses (Figure 1).

i14 and the Laplace 3B architecture

Laplace 3B is the 24-layer i14 decoder, where every layer replaces softmax attention with Simple GLA. Figure 2 follows one layer from the input xt at the top to the output xt + 1 at the bottom. This section explains each module: normalization and convolution, the QKVG projection, the GLA mixer, and the feed-forward channel mixer.

Normalization and convolution. Each token’s residual-stream vector xt ∈ ℝD (D = 3, 072) passes through a LayerNorm and a depth-wise causal Conv1d of width k = 4 with SiLU. This gives every position a 4-gram summary before the mixer. The GLA mixer then does content-based retrieval over the whole history through its decaying state.

QKVG projection. The post-conv output goes through one fused matrix Wqkvg ∈ ℝ9, 216 × 3, 072, where 9, 216 = H × (2dk + 2dv). It splits into four per-token streams: queries qt, keys kt, values vt, and a gate gt (H = 16, dk = 96, dv = 192). The gate is used after the mixer.

GLA mixer. Each head h keeps a matrix state St(h) of size dk × dv (96 × 192), a compressed, decaying record of past key-value pairs. At each token, it updates as:

Here λh is the fixed per-head decay, and ktvt⊤ is the rank-1 outer product that writes the current key-value pair into the state. The readout queries the state:

Next, a self-augmentation step adds a gated copy of the value to each head’s output:

Here σ is the sigmoid and ⊙ is the element-wise product. The gate is the query dotted with a learned per-channel rescaling of the key, where a is the learned scale (aug_balance). At initialization, a = 0, which gives a half-strength skip of the value. The per-head outputs pass through a Head RMSNorm within each decay tier, are concatenated, gated by SiLU(gt), and projected by Wout ∈ ℝD × D back to the residual stream.

Decay schedule. The per-head decay rate λh controls how fast a head forgets past tokens. It is fixed at initialization (not learned) and set by a geometric schedule. The schedule gives the 16 heads a spread of memory lengths and defines each head’s log-decay rate γh:

Decay schedule’s reach. For this model, Tmin = 1 and Tmax = 2, 048. Head 0 therefore has λ0 = 0.5 (half-life of one token), and head 15 has λ15 ≈ 0.9997 (half-life of 2,048 tokens). Heads are grouped into tiers, each sharing a Head RMSNorm.

Channel mixer (FFN). After the attention block and its residual, a second LayerNorm feeds a GLU (SiLU) FFN with inner dimension 8,192. Its three matrices are two up-projections W1, W2 ∈ ℝ8, 192 × D and one down-projection W3 ∈ ℝD × 8, 192. A second residual follows.

The state S(h) is fixed at dk × dv = 96 × 192 per head regardless of sequence length. As a result, inference is O(1) per token, and training is O(T) rather than O(T2).

ParameterValue
Parameters3.028B total (2.718B Muon + 309.6M AdamW)
Layers24 decoder layers, D = 3, 072 hidden dim
Heads16 heads, dk = 96 (half-width Q/K), dv = 192 (full-width V)
MixerSimple GLA with fixed geometric decay (Tmin = 1, Tmax = 2, 048)
ConvDepth-wise causal Conv1d, kernel width 4, SiLU
FFNGLU (SiLU), inner dim 8,192
NormLayerNorm pre-attn + Head RMSNorm (per tier) + LayerNorm pre-FFN
Vocab50,304 (padded to multiple of 64)
Sequence2,048
Training data100B tokens, FineWeb-Edu
OptimizerMuon for 2D weight matrices; AdamW for embeddings, norms
Batch size524,288 tokens/step, cosine LR, 3,815-step warmup

Engineering challenges

Each of the three changes raised its own engineering challenge.

Challenge 1: Using native PyTorch on Trainium for GLA

On GPU, GLA runs as the fused Triton kernel fused_chunk_simple_gla from the flash-linear-attention library. The GenAIIC team re-expressed it with standard PyTorch operators running through TorchNeuron Native, as explicit loops over fixed-size chunks. The chunk count is fixed at compile time and sets the backward-unroll depth. The team uses fla_num_chunks = 16, so each chunk holds C = 128 tokens.

Within each chunk c, the intra-chunk output is masked linear attention, and the running state S adds earlier context:

The state then advances to the next chunk:

Here λC is the per-head decay compounded over the chunk. The 16 intra-chunk computations run in parallel, and only the state update is sequential (Figure 3).

Because the SBUF has 128 partitions, each 128-token chunk maps one token per partition, with no padding or cross-partition movement. This alignment increased measured throughput by 14 percent (Figure 4).

Challenge 2: Distributed Muon orthogonalization under FSDP2

Muon orthogonalizes each gradient before the update. For each of the 96 two-dimensional weight matrices (2.718 billion parameters), it runs five Newton–Schulz iterations (Algorithm 1).

The distributed problem. The Gram matrix A = XX⊤ correlates every row of the weight with every other row. Under Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP2), each of the 64 ranks holds only 1/64 of the rows. A shard-local XX⊤ therefore yields only a diagonal block and drops every cross-shard term (Figure 5).

Naive approach: Gather and broadcast. Every rank gathers the full gradient (5.44 GB), one rank runs Newton–Schulz, and it broadcasts the result. This moves 10.87 GB per step while the other 63 ranks wait.

Production approach: all_to_all transposition. In MuonFSDP2, one all_to_all gives each rank a few complete matrices, all 64 ranks run Newton–Schulz in parallel, and a second all_to_all returns the results. Per-rank traffic drops to 0.45 GB, 24 times less. Throughput rises from 73,378 to 119,934 tokens per second, 1.63 times higher, with a bit-identical loss curve (Figure 6).

Communication cost. Newton–Schulz is only about 2 percent of the FLOPs in a training step (1.95 × 1014 of 9.53 × 1015), so communication was the bottleneck. Over NeuronLink-v3 at 1.28 TB/s, the 0.45 GB exchange takes under 0.4 ms of the roughly 4.4-second step.

Challenge 3: Backward-pass unrolling for a sequential recurrence

The backward pass differentiates through all 16 sequential state updates. On GPU, autograd builds this graph at runtime. On Trainium2, the compiler must see the whole unrolled 16-step graph in advance, which creates three constraints.

Graph depth grows with chunk count: at 32 chunks (C = 64), the graph overflowed the scheduler. Per-chunk memory grows with chunk size: at 8 chunks (C = 256), intermediates spilled into HBM. Every shape is fixed at trace time, so each loop intermediate needs its own static allocation.

Sixteen chunks (C = 128) satisfy all three: the unroll fits the scheduler, intermediates stay on chip, and tiles align with the 128 SBUF partitions.

Training results

The GenAIIC team trained Laplace 3B on one trn2.48xlarge instance using all 64 logical NeuronCores and the all_to_all Muon path. The full recipe is 190,735 steps (100 billion FineWeb-Edu tokens). The following results are through step 84,210, about 44 billion tokens.

Throughput. After compilation warmup, throughput settles at roughly 120,000 tokens per second and holds there through step 84,210.

Loss and gradient stability. The loss (Figure 7a) drops smoothly from about 11.4 to 2.3729 at step 84,210. The gradient norm (Figure 7b) shows the expected early spike then a steady decline to about 0.05, with no post-warmup spikes, divergence, or NaN/Inf values.

Inference optimization on Trainium2

Through an unmodified vLLM engine, the GenAIIC team served 11,544 output tokens per second at 1,280 concurrent sequences on one trn2.48xlarge instance.

Constant serving state. The 29.5 MB recurrent state per sequence is roughly 82 times smaller than a comparable KV cache at 8,192 tokens. Increasing the prompt from 2,048 to 8,192 tokens added only 0.5% to the cost per output token.

Unmodified vLLM. A wrapper replaces one attribute per decoder layer, the token mixer, to read and write the recurrent state in the vLLM pool. Because the model declares itself attention-free, vLLM allocates one fixed page per sequence. Outputs matched the i14 reference token for token (48/48 steps on 3/3 prompts in BF16).

Finding the bottleneck. A linear fit of decode time against the number of decoder layers L gives:

At L = 24, that is 168.1 ms per step, 96.9 percent of it inside the decoder layers. The large projections cost 13.27 ms, near the 12 ms HBM-streaming floor. Most time went to small operators dispatched one at a time under eager PyTorch.

Scaling to a full instance. Without tensor parallelism, throughput scales through replicas, with one engine and 20 sequences per logical NeuronCore. Eager throughput grew from 133 output tokens per second on one replica to 6,772 on 64, where host CPU usage reached 82 percent. Compiling the decode step removed per-operator dispatch and raised throughput 1.7 times, to 11,544 (Figure 8).

What fixed-batch benchmarks hide. Under real traffic, each new decode batch width is a separately compiled shape whose first use costs about 11 seconds. These steps were only 1.1 percent of the total but consumed 47.5 percent of decode time. Padding to fixed widths removed this cost with bit-exact results. Compiled decode then improved per-replica throughput 3.52 times under staggered arrivals, compared with 1.46 times on fixed batches. Because BF16 reassociation makes compiled output differ slightly from eager, use eager decode when exact reproducibility matters.

Key takeaways

The project produced lessons across both training and inference:

  • Native PyTorch can support custom architectures on Trainium2. i14 retained the GLA architecture and used TorchNeuron Native for the final implementation.
  • Communication design matters for custom optimizers. The Muon all_to_all design reduced per-rank traffic by 24 times and increased training throughput by 1.63 times.
  • Fixed state keeps inference memory predictable. Each sequence uses 29.5 MB regardless of context length.
  • Profile before compiling. Operator dispatch, rather than arithmetic or HBM bandwidth, accounted for most decode time.
  • Benchmark realistic arrival patterns. Fixed batches hid the cost of compiling new shapes for changing batch widths.

Conclusion

Laplace 3B shows that AWS Trainium2 can support model architectures beyond standard transformers. Using native PyTorch through TorchNeuron Native and the AWS Neuron SDK, i14 trained and served its GLA-based model while preserving a fixed recurrent state.

For agentic systems, this changes a basic serving constraint. Longer histories don’t require a larger per-sequence state, which can help teams retain more context while keeping memory use predictable.

If growing context is increasing serving cost, reducing concurrency, or limiting agent memory, try i14 or contact your AWS account team to evaluate Laplace 3B on AWS Trainium2.

entries.title: Work management context for AI agents with Smartsheet MCP on AWS
entries.summary: The Smartsheet Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server lets AI agents read, update, and act on live work management data. This post shows two ways to connect it on AWS: Amazon Quick for business teams and Kiro for developers, so your agents can work with Smartsheet without switching tools.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Work management context for AI agents with Smartsheet MCP on AWS

AI agents are most useful when they can act on the real work happening across your organization. Work management involves complex, cross-functional tasks such as updating project timelines, reassigning tasks, and surfacing status. AI agents can support you with these without anyone switching tools. Smartsheet, the work management platform for managing projects, portfolios, and operations, has launched a generally available Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server.

With the Smartsheet MCP Server, AI assistants can read, write, and manage Smartsheet data through a standardized protocol. The protocol spans more than 40 tools for exploring, creating, and managing sheets, rows, columns, and automations. You can update task statuses, create rows, and modify project structure directly through natural language.

In this post, we walk through two ways you can connect it to your existing workflows. Amazon Quick is an agentic AI workspace built for business users, project managers, and operations teams. They can ask questions, update sheets, and build dashboards through natural language without writing code. Kiro is an agentic IDE where developers connect to Smartsheet through MCP to reference project specs, update task status, and track dependencies without leaving their coding workflow.

Architecture overview

The following diagram shows how the Smartsheet MCP Server sits as the central integration layer connecting to AWS services. Amazon Quick and Kiro connect directly as MCP clients.

Amazon Quick serves knowledge workers, project managers, and operations teams who want to query, update, and automate Smartsheet through natural language. With Kiro, developers can reference project specs, update task status, and track dependencies without leaving their coding workflow.

The following architecture diagram illustrates these integration paths: the Smartsheet MCP Server in the center, with Amazon Quick and Kiro as MCP clients on the left, and Smartsheet’s API and data layer on the right.

Sprint management with Amazon Quick and Kiro

Consider a software engineering team that tracks their sprint in Smartsheet. Tasks, owners, statuses, and blockers all live in a project sheet. Here’s what each path looks like for the same team:

When a user such as a project manager wants to check which sprint tasks are blocked this week, they can ask Amazon Quick through natural language. The Amazon Quick chat agent queries the Smartsheet MCP Server, pulls the relevant rows, and surfaces a summary with owner names and due dates. The response is generated from live Smartsheet data without building a report or dashboard.

For developers who are fixing bugs or working through features, they can ask Kiro to pull the current sprint sheet and show them the open backend tasks assigned to them. Kiro queries Smartsheet through MCP and surfaces the list inline. When the fix is committed, a Kiro hook automatically updates the corresponding row status to Complete.

Prerequisites

Smartsheet MCP Server delivers precisely structured context, including row relationships, column types, cell history, and comments. This produces token-efficient payload sizes rather than returning raw API payloads. This engineering decision compounds into reduced cost and improved latency at scale when running hundreds of AI-assisted queries across a project portfolio. To learn how Smartsheet built their remote MCP server on AWS, see How Smartsheet built a remote MCP server on AWS.

Before connecting the Smartsheet MCP Server to Amazon Quick and Kiro, verify that you have the following in place:

  • An active AWS account with appropriate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions for the service you’re connecting (Amazon Quick, or Kiro)
  • A Smartsheet account on a Business, Enterprise, or AWM plan.
  • A Smartsheet Personal Access Token, or OAuth credentials if your client supports the OAuth flow.
  • For Amazon Quick: Author or higher permissions in your Amazon Quick account.
  • For Kiro: Kiro IDE installed from kiro.dev with 
    Node.js
    available in your environment.

The Smartsheet MCP Server is available at three regional endpoints. It uses Streamable HTTP transport (MCP spec versions 2025-06-18 and 2025-03-26) and is authenticated with either OAuth 2.0 or a Personal Access Token.

  • Commercial US: https://mcp.smartsheet.com.
  • EU: https://mcp.smartsheet.eu.
  • AU: https://mcp.smartsheet.au.

Both options expose the same Smartsheet toolset. The right choice depends on where your work gets done:

Choose Amazon Quick if you need a fully managed, organization-wide solution your whole team can use: no app registration, only pre-built OAuth, and it scales across knowledge workers in your enterprise.

Choose Kiro if you’re a developer who wants something lightweight: no infrastructure, only a config file and a personal access token, scoped to your own workflow.

Amazon Quick integration

Amazon Quick includes Smartsheet as a pre-built connector in its directory. That means reading project status, updating rows, creating discussions, and surfacing risks, all in the same interface your business users already work in.

Amazon Quick makes that integration available across the organization, from project managers and operations teams to business users who manage work in Smartsheet.

To add the Quick integration:

  • In the Amazon Quick console, navigate to Connectors and find Smartsheet in the directory.
  • Select the Smartsheet connector tile.
  • Enter the following integration details:
    • Name – Descriptive name for your Smartsheet integration.
    • Keep the Connection type and Auth configuration settings as is.
    • Base URL – https://mcp.smartsheet.com.
    • Client ID – App client ID from your Smartsheet Developer Tools app registration.
    • Client Secret – App secret from your Smartsheet Developer Tools app registration.
    • Token URL – https://api.smartsheet.com/2.0/token.
    • Auth URL – https://app.smartsheet.com/b/authorize.
  • Choose Next.
  • On the Manage Tools & Permissions page, you see a list of available tools. Choose Next.
  • On the Publish page, choose who can access this connection, and then choose Publish.
  • Choose Next.

After you’re connected, your Amazon Quick chat agent can work with Smartsheet data through natural language:

  • “What projects in our portfolio are currently At Risk?”
  • “Update the status of the authentication task in the Backend API sheet to Complete.”
  • “Create a summary of all overdue items across the Q3 Roadmap and send it to the team.”

Kiro integration

Kiro is the right path when developers want Smartsheet project context available directly in their development environment, alongside their code, without context-switching.

Kiro is built around spec-driven development. It turns high-level prompts into structured specs, then into working code, docs, and tests. MCP servers are how Kiro gets real-world context by connecting to documentation, databases, APIs, and enterprise systems to ground its agent in live data rather than training-time knowledge.

A Kiro feature called powers is a one-click installable bundle that packages a curated MCP server with steering files and hooks. It gives the Kiro coding agent a new capability out of the box. For Smartsheet, configuring the connection takes a single JSON configuration block and from that point, the Kiro agent can reference live project data as part of a development workflow.

To connect the Smartsheet MCP Server to Kiro, add it to your Kiro MCP configuration (

.kiro/settings/mcp.json
for workspace scope). For a full walkthrough, see Getting Started with Kiro and MCP Servers:

This configuration uses the Personal Access Token (API key) approach. For production deployments, OAuth is recommended.

Set 

SMARTSHEET_API_TOKEN
to your Smartsheet Personal Access Token in your environment. Kiro loads MCP servers as background processes on startup. After it’s initialized, Smartsheet tools are available to the Kiro agent across all modes: chat, spec planning, and hooks-based automation. Full details in the Smartsheet MCP Server Documentation.

From there, Kiro can reference Smartsheet data as part of development workflows:

  • “Check the Backend API project sheet for any open bugs and generate a prioritized fix list.”
  • “Pull the Q3 Roadmap sheet and create a spec for the features marked In Progress.”

Enterprise governance

For builders deploying in regulated or enterprise environments, the Smartsheet MCP Server security model is built on the same infrastructure and permissions layer as the Smartsheet REST API. It’s not a new trust boundary:

  • OAuth 2.0 and Personal Access Token authentication: choose the auth method supported by your MCP client.
  • User-level permission enforcement: agents can only access data the authenticated user has permission to see. No privilege escalation through natural language prompts.
  • Organization-level AI controls: system administrators can turn on or off AI features globally. Write-tool access is configurable by user group.
  • Streamable HTTP transport: firewall allowlisting is done by fully qualified domain name (FQDN) (mcp.smartsheet.com), not IP address.

For compliance architects, the MCP Server doesn’t store prompts, and prompt content stays between the AI client and the model. Smartsheet sees only the structured tool calls and their results.

Clean up

If you followed this walkthrough and want to remove the integration afterward, here’s how to undo each path:

Amazon Quick

  • In the Amazon Quick console, navigate to Connectors.
  • Select your Smartsheet connector.
  • Choose Delete to remove the connection. This revokes the OAuth token and stops agent access to Smartsheet data.

Kiro

  • Open your MCP configuration file (
    .kiro/settings/mcp.json
    ).
  • Remove the 
    smartsheet-us
    entry from the 
    mcpServers
    object.
  • Restart Kiro to unload the server.

Next steps

For background on how the server works, see How Smartsheet built a remote MCP server on AWS. After you’ve connected the Smartsheet MCP Server to your system of choice, here are four actions we recommend trying:

You can ask the chat agent to monitor your active project sheets, identify rows marked Blocked or At Risk. You can also ask to annotate projects with a discussion comment, and deliver a structured summary to your team through your preferred channel. This would be an example workflow that chains 

get_sheet_summary
, 
search
, and 
create_discussion_on_row
.

The agent can also retrieve data through the Smartsheet MCP Server to reconcile task statuses between your issue tracker and your Smartsheet project plan. It can flag drift between the two, and update the affected rows, using 

get_sheet_summary
, 
get_columns
, 
update_rows
, and 
create_discussion_on_row
in sequence.

You can also try to aggregate project health signals across your reports and dashboards. You can use it to produce a structured briefing without manual data gathering, drawing on 

list_reports
, 
get_report
, 
list_dashboards
, 
get_dashboard
, and 
search
.

Lastly, you can use the agent to follow every write with a discussion comment explaining what changed and why. This creates a human-readable audit trail inside Smartsheet through the combination of 

update_rows
and 
create_discussion_on_row
.

All four patterns work across the preceding paths: Amazon Quick for business-user-facing workflows, and Kiro for developer-initiated actions.

Building something with Smartsheet MCP and AWS? Share what you’re working on in the comments, or connect with us in the Smartsheet Developer Community.

entries.title: From data to decisions: Conversational supply chain intelligence with Amazon Quick and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
entries.summary: Enterprise supply chains are data-rich but insight-poor, with the data to decide scattered across ERP, monitoring, procurement, and email. This post shows how Amazon Bedrock AgentCore exposes those systems as a governed tool layer, and how Amazon Quick turns them into one conversational experience for business users, with a deploy-it-yourself walkthrough.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

From data to decisions: Conversational supply chain intelligence with Amazon Quick and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

Giving supply chain teams direct access to the systems behind their decisions.

Every supply chain generates constant signals: orders in approval, shifting lead times, slowing ports, drifting prices, disruptions. The problem isn’t scarce data. It’s the distance between the data and the decision-maker.

Answering “which top-revenue SKUs are exposed to the current port closure, and what will it cost?” used to mean knowing which system held each piece and stitching them together by hand while the domain expert waited.

Could that manager instead ask in plain language and get an actionable, cross-system answer in seconds? Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is the intelligence layer, exposing enterprise Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers as a composable tool layer. Amazon Quick turns that into action for personas with no setup. Answers come from live systems of record and grounded documents, not model recall, and every change waits for a named human. In this post, we walk through this pattern end to end, from a conversational walkthrough in Amazon Quick to the AgentCore tool layer behind it, and we show you how to deploy it yourself.

The problem: Data-rich, insight-poor

Each question needs its own tool: inventory from the enterprise resource planning (ERP) system, disruptions from email or news, a request for quotation (RFQ) from procurement, and compliance from a checklist. Correlating is manual.

A day in the life

A manager’s morning traditionally spans the ERP (inventory exceptions), monitoring tool (alerts), procurement (alternatives), email (RFQ), and a tracker: 45–60 minutes across five systems with a dozen-plus context switches.

Conversationally it’s three prompts in one tool, “Any critical disruptions affecting my top-revenue SKUs?” → “Assess the TechComp halt and issue an emergency RFQ to approved alternatives” → “Looks good. Send it.”, in minutes.

Deep dive: Supply chain scenario walkthrough

The following five steps follow one disruption from detection to an approved emergency RFQ, all in a single Amazon Quick conversation.

Step 1: Discovery – “What tools do I have?”

The user asks “What supply chain tools do I have?” and Amazon Quick lists the supply chain MCP servers published in AWS Agent Registry. Because an administrator has turned on the registry integration, the four business MCP servers already appear as connector cards, with connection details pre-populated and no URLs to enter by hand. The orchestration agent is added as its own MCP connector.

Step 2: Querying – “Show me active disruptions”

“Check active supply disruptions” calls the Disruption Alerts MCP (

assess_disruption_impact
): three disruptions with severity, region, and SKU counts. How we solve it: Quick routes the request through AgentCore to the MCP server, which queries backend monitoring and returns a structured result, no dashboard or export.

Step 3: Drill-down – “Assess the critical one”

The user opens the TechComp Production Halt. 

assess_disruption_impact(disruption_id="DISR-002")
correlates order, customer, and inventory data: $750K at risk, 23 orders, three days of supply. How we solve it: one MCP tool call fans out across systems of record, so the manager gets a consolidated impact read without touching the ERP.

Step 4: Action – “Get mitigation recommendations”

The user asks for mitigation. 

recommend_mitigation(disruption_id="DISR-002")
chains the Governance MCP (verify approved alternatives) and Quoting MCP (contract-aligned quote), one flow from one request. How we solve it: the agent plans and sequences the calls, so a single ask spans disruption, governance, and quoting with no manual hand-offs.

Step 5: Automated follow-up

The user then sets up proactive monitoring (“Alert me every morning if there’s a new critical disruption”). The same flow can run unattended from an inbound supplier email. How we solve it: the same agent and tools run on a schedule or email trigger, posting review-ready cards to the Activity Feed for a person to approve.

Put end to end, those five steps are a single runtime sequence:

Solution architecture

That’s the experience. Here’s how it is built: the pattern separates the intelligence layer from the interface layer, so each evolves independently, with Amazon Quick as the interface and AgentCore as the intelligence.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: The intelligence layer

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a modular agentic platform for building, deploying, and operating agents securely at scale. It offers more than we use here. Four of its services are relevant to this pattern:

  • Runtime – Serverless hosting for MCP servers and agents, with session isolation and built-in identity.
  • Gateway – Turns APIs, AWS Lambda functions, and services into MCP-compatible tools behind a secure managed endpoint, standardizing tool access. Reasoning is the calling agent’s.
  • Identity – Authentication and credential management, compatible with existing identity providers.
  • Policy – Deterministic authorization rules, authored in natural language or Cedar, that intercept every tool call before execution, keeping an agent in its lane on procurement and financial data.

The MCP protocol: How tools communicate

MCP is an open standard for how AI models interact with external tools. Each server exposes tools with typed parameters:

This means:

  • AI clients (Quick, custom agents, other MCP apps) can consume the same servers.
  • Backends (SAP, Oracle, custom microservices) can be wrapped as an MCP server.
  • Tool discovery is automatic. Clients query the registry for schemas at runtime.

AWS Agent Registry: The discovery layer

The registry is the governed discovery layer: a publisher submits a record, a curator approves it, and only then is it discoverable through hybrid search, browsing, or the registry’s MCP endpoint. One scale reality worth noting: because schemas are discovered at runtime, treat each as a contract, versioning new alongside old for breaking changes.

Multi-step orchestration

The reasoning layer is an agent on AgentCore Runtime, an agent record at its direct invocation URL through a Custom MCP connector, with no Lambda or gateway. Here, it’s the Order Fulfillment Agent. Given one request it plans which tools to call and in what order:

Security and governance architecture

Every tool call passes through the same AgentCore control set before it reaches a backend.

The MCP servers in this pattern

sc-quoting-gateway
)		 Quote generation, pricing rules, validation“Contract-aligned quote for 500 units of SKU-A”

Invoice Processing (

Disruption Alerts (

)		 Active disruptions, severity, impact assessments, mitigation“Critical disruptions affecting our APAC suppliers?”
Order Fulfillment Agent (
sc-order-fulfillment-agent
)		 Multi-step orchestration across all four business MCPs (AgentCore Runtime, direct invocation URL)“A supplier went down, find alternatives, check compliance, issue an RFQ”

Amazon Quick: The enterprise AI assistant

Amazon Quick puts AgentCore tools before business users through chat, agents, the Activity Feed, and automated workflows, with no technical setup.

Key components used

Agent Registry connectionSurfaces MCP servers as connectorsAdmin links the registry once. Records become connector cards
Quick AgentOne SC agent that adapts to roleTailors to persona (manager, procurement, analyst)

SchedulesRecurring natural-language automationFor example, “every morning”

Structured data connectorsQuery operational recordsQuick queries Space datasets (orders, inventory, suppliers, contracts) for the MCP rule check
Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) knowledge baseRetrieval over documentsInvoices, contracts, policies in an S3 knowledge base, grounding answers through Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)
CRM connector (optional)Reads customer records (optional)CRM (for example, Salesforce) accounts, opportunities, contacts. Can also load into datasets

Automated Activity Feed and proactive monitoring

The Activity Feed is the proactive surface of Amazon Quick, a unified inbox where agents post results, alerts, and recommendations. Feed items are:

  • Actionable, each carries context and next-step actions.
  • AI-triaged, with priority indicators (Reply needed, Follow up, Deadline).
  • Cross-source, spanning email, schedules, agent runs, and external systems.
  • Human-in-the-loop, where agents propose and humans decide.

How automated monitoring works

AgentCore tools plus the proactive capabilities of Amazon Quick give two paths, time-based and email-driven, through a common trigger → agent → output pipeline.

Use case: Validate supplier responses from email

Suppliers reply to an emergency RFQ by email with pricing. The agent validates each (approved supplier? within guidelines?) and stages the result. It does not author a quote, pick a winner, or issue a purchase order (PO).

Phase 1: Setup (one-time, approximately 5 minutes)

  • Connect Outlook: in Amazon Quick, choose Settings → Connections → Add Outlook.
  • Configure Activity Feed: turn on email monitoring in feed preferences.
  • Create SC Agent: build an agent with these instructions:
  • Create Schedule: “Every 2 hours during business hours, check for new supplier replies and validate them.”

Phase 2: Runtime (fully automated)

The feed card carries the validation results and decision-relevant facts:

Supplier Response: Ready for ReviewDetails
SupplierTechSupply Co, ✅ approved vendor
SKU / Qty / PriceMCU-7200 · 10,000 units · $2.45/unit
Price check✅ within purchasing guidelines
ActionsSelect for PO · Compare responses · Reject

Phase 3: Human-in-the-loop

The reviewer compares validated responses and either selects a supplier and issues the PO, or rejects with a logged reason. Selection and the PO stay with a person.

Use case: Proactive disruption monitoring

Schedule-triggered, the same pattern applies: a daily 8:30 AM agent checks for new critical or high-severity disruptions, assesses impact, flags anything under seven days of supply as URGENT, and posts an alert card with an Issue Emergency RFQ action.

Where this fits alongside traditional BI

DimensionTraditional business intelligence (BI) / dashboardsAgentCore + Amazon Quick
Access modelNavigate, log in, find the dashboard/reportAsk in natural language. The system finds the source
Time to insightMinutes to hours (find → filter → export → correlate)Seconds (ask → answer with cross-system context)
Multi-system correlationManual: 3-4 tabs, copy-pasteAutomatic: the agent orchestrates across MCP servers from one query
Action gapInsight in one tool → switch → act in anotherInsight → action in the same conversation
Setup costWeeks/months (dashboard design, ETL, permissions, training)Minutes to connect, once your MCP servers exist
Run costFixed: pipelines cost the same whether or not anyone asksUsage-based: serverless scales to zero, cost tracks questions (Lambda + agent tokens)
Trust & accuracyAs fresh as the last ETL loadComputed live from systems of record and grounded docs, every write human-gated

This isn’t a “replace everything” argument. Dashboards remain superior for trend visualization, collaborative analysis, regulatory reporting, and exploratory analysis. Use conversational AI for real-time operational decisions and BI for strategic analysis. They complement, not compete.

Personas and use cases

One Quick Agent serves all three personas: the manager maintains continuity, procurement sources with compliance-awareness, the analyst correlates signals. Persona also bounds reach, through row/column-level security and per-persona MCP-tool scoping, so procurement does not see finance data.

SC ManagerEmergency procurementGovernance → Quoting MCPVerified alternatives + RFQ, one flow
ProcurementSupplier verification, budget authorityGovernance MCPApproval, compliance, limits
ProcurementRFQ generation and response validationQuoting MCPRFQ issued + responses validated
Ops AnalystCross-system correlationSC Operations AgentMulti-MCP reasoning, one query
Ops AnalystPayment queue, audit, disruption trendsInvoice / Governance MCPAP aging, audit log, patterns

Getting started

Deploying the pattern takes three phases: provision the infrastructure, connect Amazon Quick to your data and the registry, and turn on monitoring.

Prerequisites

Before you begin:

  • An AWS account with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and AWS Agent Registry.
  • AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) v2, AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM) CLI, and Docker (the agent runs as an arm64 container).
  • Python 3.12 or later, with Boto3 1.43.94 or later for the registry step.
  • Active credentials with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to deploy and register (
    aws sts get-caller-identity
    returns the target account).
  • Data layer: a database (Snowflake, PostgreSQL/RDS, or a SQLAlchemy engine), an Amazon S3 bucket, optionally a Salesforce org.
  • Amazon Quick set up for your organization.
  • (Optional) An Outlook account for email automation.

Setup uses two surfaces, so each of the following steps names where it happens: the Amazon Quick web console in a browser (Amazon Quick Sight permissions, Agent Registry linking, connectors, and agent settings) and the Quick Desktop App (connecting Outlook for email automation). The conversational experience in the Desktop App comes last, once setup is done.

Deploy the infrastructure

Everything is open source and scripted: clone the quick-for-supply-chain example in the aws-samples/sample-amazon-quick-suite-knowledge-hub repository and follow its 

README.md
, or point a coding agent like Kiro at it.

The 

README.md
covers three phases. Phase 1 deploys the AgentCore stack: the identity layer (an Amazon Cognito user pool and app client, authorization-code OAuth flow, plus a test user), four business-rule MCP servers (each an AWS Lambda function fronted by its own AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, using 
CUSTOM_JWT
authorization), the gateway targets mapping the tools of each Lambda function, and 
sc-order-fulfillment-agent
on AgentCore Runtime as a container, with least-privilege IAM roles. Phase 2 uploads the synthetic dataset to Amazon S3. Phase 3 verifies gateways and runtime are Ready. Six Agent Registry records are approved.

Grant Amazon Quick access to your data

In the Amazon Quick web console (browser): grant Amazon Quick access from the Amazon Quick Sight admin page (Manage Quick Sight → Security and permissions) to both the S3 bucket and Amazon Athena, since each table is served through an Athena source over an AWS Glue database. Without the Athena grant, dataset creation fails.

Link the registry and create connectors

Linking the registry is one-time and administrator-level. Creating a connector is per-user. Both happen in the Amazon Quick console. See the AWS Agent Registry integration guide.

Link the registry (administrator, one-time)

An administrator links one Agent Registry to the Quick account. In the Amazon Quick web console (admin): go to Manage account → Permissions → AWS Agent Registry and turn on the registry (

sc-supply-chain-registry
, one per account). Only registries in your account and Region, agent-registry namespace, AWS_IAM (SigV4) authorization, and READY status appear. The Quick-managed service role links it.

Create a connector

After the registry is linked, approved MCP server records become connector cards: the four business MCPs as cards, the order-fulfillment agent added manually. At scale, federate connector authentication through your identity provider and provision connectors to groups, with the Cognito user pool as the seam.

In the Amazon Quick web console (per user): the four cards appear on the Connectors page (

sc-quoting-mcp
, 
sc-governance-mcp
, 
sc-invoice-processing-mcp
, 
sc-disruption-alert-mcp
). Authenticate through the OAuth authorization-code flow (
OAUTH2_AUTHORIZATION_CODE
) with client ID, secret, and token, authorization, and redirect URLs from the deploy script. Sign in as the test user, turn on tools, create and share.

Registry-sourced connectors are Custom MCP connectors (relevant for custom permissions). Removing the link later doesn’t delete connectors already created.

Add the order-fulfillment agent connector

In the Amazon Quick web console: because it is an agent record, create its connector manually (Connectors → Create for your team → Model Context Protocol → Create new): name it 

sc-order-fulfillment-agent
, point it at the AgentCore Runtime direct invocation URL from the deploy script, complete the same OAuth sign-in, create and share.

Attach the connectors to your agent

The deployment creates the Supply Chain agent: a Quick Space, imported datasets and S3 knowledge base, and the agent with instructions, starter prompts, and welcome message. What remains is attaching the connectors.

In the Amazon Quick web console (agent settings): open the deployment-created Supply Chain agent (default id 

sc-supply-chain-agent
) and attach all five connectors (four business MCPs plus 
sc-order-fulfillment-agent
), or pass the five connector IDs to the setup script.

Set up proactive monitoring

To make it proactive, Quick runs the same agent on a schedule or on incoming email and posts results to the Activity Feed. Both paths reuse the agent and tools you configured.

In the Quick Desktop App (Settings → Connections): connect Outlook and turn on email monitoring. Then, in Quick Chat, create two natural-language schedules, time-based (“Every morning, check for new critical disruptions”) and email-driven (“Every two hours in business hours, check supplier replies and validate”). The agent extracts pricing, runs the checks, and posts a card.

Try it in Amazon Quick

With the agent and connectors ready, ask in natural language in Amazon Quick Chat. Each prompt shows the data-then-rules pattern.

Ask Amazon QuickWhat you get
“What supply chain tools do I have?”The five MCP connectors (quoting, governance, invoice, disruption alerts, order-fulfillment agent), with status.
“Show me active supply disruptions.”Active disruptions with severity, region, SKU counts (Disruption Alerts MCP).
“Assess the impact of the TechComp production halt.”Revenue at risk, affected orders, days of supply, from your datasets.
“Is this supplier an approved vendor, and do we have budget authority for a $72,000 PO?”An approval from the Governance MCP (vendor status, budget authority, compliance).
“Generate a contract-aligned quote for 1,000 units for this customer.”A contract-aligned quote from the Quoting MCP, as a branded document.
“A supplier just went down. Find alternatives, verify compliance, and issue an emergency RFQ.”The Order Fulfillment Agent chains disruption, governance, and quoting MCPs into one recommendation.

Conclusion

AgentCore and Amazon Quick are a repeatable enterprise-AI pattern: separate intelligence from interface. AgentCore turns fragmented backends into a composable, governed, AI-accessible layer through standard MCP interfaces. Amazon Quick democratizes access in natural language.

The gain is the collapsed decision chain: detect, research, decide, act, and log once spanned five tools, now one conversation. The AI researches, correlates, validates. The person decides. Every call is authenticated, authorized, policy-checked, and audited, and a 45-60 minute routine across five systems can collapse to minutes.

That is the shift from data-rich, insight-poor to data-rich, decision-ready. Start with one MCP server and one persona. The registry grows and the experience stays the same.

entries.title: Fine-tuning GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
entries.summary: Learn how we fine-tuned GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, and how to decide between supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning with GRPO. SFT took reasoning-language accuracy from 22% to 100%, and GRPO added measurable gains where headroom existed.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Fine-tuning GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod

GPT-OSS-20B is an open-weight reasoning model that thinks in English. Ask it to reason in French, German, Spanish, or Italian and it acknowledges the instruction, then produces its chain-of-thought in English anyway. On a 50-example multilingual reasoning test, the base model reasoned in the correct target language only 22 percent of the time. That 22 percent was almost entirely the English examples (English 100 percent, French 0 percent, German 10 percent, Spanish 0 percent, Italian 0 percent).

For teams deploying reasoning models for non-English users, that gap matters. A user who asks a question in French expects the model to reason and answer in French, not to switch to English mid-thought. Closing that gap is a fine-tuning problem. It raises a question every team faces once they start customizing open-weight models: supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), or both?

In this post, we walk through how we fine-tuned GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod. We show when SFT alone was sufficient and when GRPO added measurable value on top. To understand more broadly when GRPO helps, we also ran a controlled Qwen2.5-7B experiment across two tasks with different capability gaps. The short answer: SFT does most of the work, GRPO refines when there is headroom to refine, and matching the technique to the capability gap is what decides the outcome.

Solution overview

This section covers the multilingual reasoning task and dataset, how SFT and GRPO complement each other, and the training stack we ran on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod.

The task and dataset

The dataset is 

HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking
— a chain-of-thought reasoning dataset translated into French, Spanish, German, and Italian alongside English, roughly 949 training and 50 validation examples. The model receives a 
reasoning language:
system-prompt instruction and must both reason and answer in that target language, overriding its strong English prior. The evaluation is 50 test cases: 10 math/logic problems across 5 languages (EN/FR/DE/ES/IT).

Two metrics matter:

  • Reasoning-language correct – is the chain-of-thought in the requested language?
  • Answer-language correct – is the final answer in the requested language?

How SFT and GRPO fit together

The clearest way to think about the two techniques: SFT teaches a behavior the model doesn’t have. GRPO optimizes a behavior the model can already sometimes produce. GRPO works by sampling a group of responses per prompt and pushing the policy toward the above-average ones. If the desired behavior has zero probability in the base distribution, there is very little for GRPO to reinforce. That single idea explains almost every result in this post.

The training stack

We ran on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod with Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) orchestration. For the initial SFT and GRPO runs on GPT-OSS-20B, we used the PyTorch TRL library. For the Qwen control experiment, we switched to veRL as the trainer, with Ray and KubeRay for distributed orchestration and vLLM for fast rollout generation. Checkpoints and datasets lived on Amazon FSx for Lustre, and the inter-node fabric used Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA). All fine-tuning used Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), which is parameter-efficient and well-suited to both SFT and GRPO.

The following diagram shows the training data path end-to-end. A submission from the user lands on the Amazon EKS control plane of the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster. Amazon EKS schedules a Ray head pod plus worker pods that run the veRL trainer and vLLM rollout workers. Both sets of pods mount Amazon FSx for Lustre for the base model, training data, and checkpoints. Inter-node collectives use EFA. Rollouts stream from vLLM back to the veRL trainer, and the trainer writes checkpoints back to Amazon FSx for Lustre.

The following describes each hop in more detail. The submitter starts the run from Amazon SageMaker Studio or the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI). The Amazon EKS control plane on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod places pods on GPU nodes and starts a Ray head with worker pods for the veRL trainer and the vLLM rollout workers. Amazon FSx for Lustre provides shared, high-throughput storage for the base model, the training data, and the checkpoints.
