When training completes, the trainer writes the LoRA adapter back to Amazon FSx for Lustre for downstream evaluation or serving.

Prerequisites

To follow along, you need:

  • An Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster with Amazon EKS orchestration. GPT-OSS SFT used 4× ml.g6e.12xlarge (16× L40S 48GB). The Qwen control used 2× g6e.48xlarge (16× L40S).
  • An Amazon FSx for Lustre file system mounted on the cluster with a 
    PersistentVolumeClaim
    named 
    fsx-claim
    at 
    /fsx
    .
  • EFA-enabled instances and a working NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) and 
    aws-ofi-nccl
    stack for multi-node SFT.
  • A container registry such as Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) to hold the training image built from the reference repository.
  • A HuggingFace access token for 
    openai/gpt-oss-20b
    and the 
    HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking
    dataset.
  • The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), 
    kubectl
    , 
    docker
    , and 
    envsubst
    available on your workstation.

Set up the training environment

All of the commands, manifests, and scripts referenced below live in the awsome-distributed-ai GitHub repository under 

3.test_cases/pytorch/trl/gpt-oss-lora-grpo/
. Clone the repository and change into the test case directory:

Copy the environment template, then edit 

env_vars
to set your ECR registry, image name, tag, and HuggingFace token:

Build the training image and push it to your registry. The image bundles PyTorch, TRL, HuggingFace Transformers, PEFT, and the training and inference scripts:

Point 

kubectl
at your cluster and apply the FSx storage manager pod. The storage manager gives you a shell into the shared file system for checkpoint conversion and eval-log inspection:

Fine-tune GPT-OSS-20B with SFT and LoRA

We begin by measuring the base model, then configure the SFT run and examine the results.

The base-model gap

Base GPT-OSS-20B on the 50-case eval scored 22 percent reasoning-language correct (11/50). Per-language: English 100 percent, French 0 percent, German 10 percent, Spanish 0 percent, Italian 0 percent. The model defaults to English reasoning regardless of the instruction.

SFT configuration

The SFT setup used LoRA r=8, α=16, trained for 1,000 steps on 4× ml.g6e.12xlarge (16× L40S 48GB) with Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) full-shard, bf16 precision, and gradient checkpointing. The job runs as an elastic 

HyperPodPyTorchJob
managed by Kueue, launched with 
hyperpodrun
.

Apply the SFT manifest:

Watch training progress:

Loss and gradient norm print each step. A healthy run looks like this:

When training completes, convert the FSDP checkpoint to the Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) format that TRL’s GRPO trainer and the inference scripts expect:

SFT results and the staged learning curve

After SFT, the model reasons in the correct language 100 percent of the time (50/50) across all five languages. SFT learned this in two stages:

  • Around step 200, the model learned to reason in the target language (reasoning-language metric hits 100 percent).
  • Around step 1000, the model additionally learned to give the answer in the target language.

Final SFT eval (step 1000):

  • Reasoning-language correct: 100 percent (50/50).
  • Answer-language correct: 62 percent (31/50).
  • Both correct: 62 percent (31/50).
  • Per-language answer accuracy: FR 60 percent, DE 60 percent, ES 30 percent, IT 60 percent, EN 100 percent.

Takeaway: SFT is not optional here. The base model can’t follow the reasoning-language instruction at all, and SFT takes reasoning-language from 22 percent to 100 percent. The remaining gap is answer-language at 62 percent. That’s the harder half, because the final answer is short and the English prior is strongest there.

Refine answer-language with GRPO

Answer-language was the obvious target for GRPO. SFT already produced correct reasoning 100 percent of the time, and the model sometimes produced the answer in the right language, so there was a signal to reinforce.

Run GRPO on top of the SFT checkpoint

We ran GRPO with TRL’s 

GRPOTrainer
, starting from the SFT checkpoint. The setup: load the SFT LoRA, call 
merge_and_unload
, and add a new LoRA (r=8, α=16, about 0.068 percent trainable parameters, 13.6M of 20B). Training used K=8 generations per prompt, 
device_map=auto
, learning rate 1e-6, and 10 epochs. The reward function scored answer-language (±5.0), reasoning-language (±1.5), and brevity (+0.5 or −1.0), for a combined range of −7.5 to +7.0.

Launch GRPO from the converted SFT checkpoint:

GRPO writes checkpoints to 

/fsx/checkpoints/grpo-singlenode/
. Pick the best checkpoint against your held-out eval (the answer-language metric peaked early in this run) and convert it to PEFT format for inference and evaluation.

Result (from the SFT checkpoint):

  • Reasoning-language correct: 100 percent (held: GRPO didn’t break what SFT taught).
  • Answer-language correct: 62 to 70 percent (+8 points, 35/50).
  • Both correct: 70 percent.
  • Per-language answer: FR 70 percent, DE 80 percent, ES 60 percent, IT 40 percent, EN 100 percent.

GRPO delivered a real +8 point gain on the answer-language metric while holding reasoning at 100 percent. The gain came where there was headroom to gain. Answer-language was the sometimes-correct behavior that SFT had not fully converged on, and GRPO reinforced it.

Compare base, SFT, and GRPO inference side by side

To see the qualitative difference, deploy three inference pods that share the same base model but load different adapters:

Run the same French-reasoning prompt through each variant:

The base pod reasons in English despite the instruction. The SFT pod reasons in French but often answers in English. The GRPO pod reasons and answers in French. To reproduce the full 50-case eval that generated the numbers earlier, run the evaluation manifest and read the result file from the FSx storage manager:

To understand more broadly when GRPO adds value, we ran a controlled experiment on Qwen2.5-7B across two tasks with different capability gaps.

Test the pattern with a Qwen2.5-7B control

To test the “match technique to capability gap” thesis on a different model and different tasks, we ran controlled experiments on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. The first task is the same multilingual reasoning task (where headroom exists). The second task is GSM8K, where the model is already at peak accuracy. This is an internal experiment, and the public repo has not yet been released.

Infrastructure: 2× g6e.48xlarge (16× L40S), EFA 100Gbps, FSx Lustre, Ray 2.44 + KubeRay 1.4.2, veRL v0.6.1, vLLM 0.8.4.

Arms: A = base, B = SFT-only, C = SFT+GRPO.

Multilingual reasoning (50 cases)

MetricA baseB SFTC SFT+GRPOΔ GRPO
Structured format0%92%98%+6
Reasoning language0%96%98%+2
Answer language0%38%44%+6
Both correct0%38%44%+6

GSM8K, a task with no headroom

On GSM8K, base Qwen2.5-7B already scores 90.5 percent (181/200). GRPO at step 30 also scores 90.5 percent. When most sampled groups are all-correct, the group-relative advantage collapses to zero, so there is no learning signal. This is the other half of the thesis: GRPO needs headroom (pass@k >> pass@1) to have anything to optimize. No headroom means no gain.

Best practices

  • Start with SFT. GRPO cannot teach a behavior with zero base probability. It can only reinforce responses the model already sometimes produces. SFT took reasoning-language from 22 percent to 100 percent, and every GRPO win in this work was built on that SFT checkpoint.
  • Use LoRA for both SFT and GRPO. LoRA r=8/α=16 was parameter-efficient (0.068 percent trainable), and on the Qwen control it stayed numerically stable through GRPO (grad norm 0.23, about 11.7 GB per GPU). It’s a strong default when you want SFT and GRPO to share the same adapter shape.
  • Match the technique to the gap. Use SFT for missing behavior. Use GRPO for refining an existing, sometimes-correct behavior. GRPO’s realistic ceiling here was +6 to +8 points.
  • Check for reward headroom before spending GPU-hours. If most groups are all-correct (GSM8K 90.5 percent base), the group-relative advantage collapses to zero and GRPO gets no gradient. Verify there is headroom (pass@k >> pass@1) before starting a GRPO run.

Clean up resources

To avoid ongoing charges, delete the workload resources and then the underlying infrastructure:

  • Delete the training and inference pods and jobs:
  • Scale down or delete the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster or its node groups.
  • Delete the Amazon FSx for Lustre file system once you have exported any checkpoints you want to keep.
  • Delete any Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) buckets or objects used for training data or checkpoint archives.

Conclusion

We showed how to fine-tune GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, and how to decide between SFT and GRPO. SFT did most of the work: reasoning-language went from 22 percent to 100 percent. GRPO added a real, modest refinement on top (answer 62 percent to 70 percent) where headroom existed. A parallel Qwen2.5-7B control confirmed the pattern. GRPO added +6 percent on multilingual reasoning, where there was room to improve. It added no gain on GSM8K, where the model was already at peak accuracy (90.5 percent).

Decision framework:

  • Behavior the model can’t do at all: use SFT.
  • Behavior it does sometimes, with headroom: use SFT then GRPO for a few points more.
  • Model already at peak accuracy, or target has zero base probability: GRPO won’t help.

To try this yourself, walk through the test cases in the awsome-distributed-ai repository. For more on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, see the service detail page and the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod documentation. For a walkthrough of Ray on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, see the related post Running distributed training on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod with Ray and Amazon SageMaker Studio. The link will be added after that post is published. Share your results in the comments.

entries.title: How Octave built a secure multi-tenant AI foundation on Amazon Bedrock
entries.summary: Octave built a secure, multi-tenant AI foundation on Amazon Bedrock, using Cohere Embed v4 for embeddings and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for isolated agent execution, to power a Complaint Triage Assistant that searches 2 billion regulated documents without crossing tenant boundaries.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

How Octave built a secure multi-tenant AI foundation on Amazon Bedrock

In quality management for regulated industries, the institutional memory that resolves a problem is almost always buried somewhere in a customer’s history. A similar defect investigated last year, a Corrective and Preventive Action (CAPA) that fixed the root cause, an audit finding that flagged the same gap. That knowledge sits in billions of documents no human can search by semantic similarity across languages and formats, so every investigation starts from scratch. Octave Reliance has helped each organization collect documents across multiple systems to help them search more easily and keep track of everything they have. The Octave Reliance team saw unlocking this history as its single largest opportunity to help customers work faster and stay compliant. The obstacle was equally clear: complaint records, audit findings, and corrective actions carry the platform’s strictest isolation requirements, and those were exactly the records the AI would need to read. In a platform serving over 14,000 customers across medical devices, pharmaceuticals, and food manufacturing, a single inadvertent disclosure from one customer to another would carry regulatory consequences far outweighing any AI benefit.

Octave operates across 180 countries, serving more than 60% of the Global Fortune 500. Its cloud-native quality management system, Reliance, supports over 650 enterprise customers with over 40 applications, from complaint management and CAPA tracking to audit management and supplier quality. Everyone generates regulated data that AI could reason over. Each customer is a separate tenant and no data can cross a tenant boundary.

Faced with that, the Reliance team made an unusual call: rather than shipping one AI feature, it spent its first cycle building a foundation every future feature would sit on. That foundation has since cut deployment time per use case by 50 percent. If you are bringing AI to a software as a service (SaaS) platform where the data is valuable, but isolation is non-negotiable, the reasoning travels beyond quality management. In this post, we walk through the four tensions that shaped the design and the three-layer foundation Octave built with Cohere Embed v4 on Amazon Bedrock. We then follow the pipeline that embedded 2 billion documents and the Complaint Triage Assistant that proved it in production.

Why a foundation, not a feature

Envisioning workshops with AWS surfaced four high-impact use cases: complaint summarization and triage, audit readiness monitoring, incident narrative generation, and predictive quality risk scoring. They also surfaced the insight that shaped everything after dozens of applications, each with different document types and workflows. Building AI for one in a silo meant rebuilding the infrastructure for the next.

So, the team inverted the plan: build the horizontal platform first, then cut vertical feature slices into it. Complaint summarization and triage went first, to prove the architecture before the rest followed.

The four tensions

Before selecting a single model, the team spent its time on four problems that pulled in different directions. None could be traded away.

Making data available without risking inadvertent disclosure. Complaint records, CAPAs, standard operating procedures (SOPs), and audit findings belong to one tenant and must be unreachable by another. Not even an errant AI query could cross. Vector store, retrieval logic, and generation context all had to be scoped to a single tenant.

Executing agents in isolation. The permissions governing an agent’s tools, data stores, and model endpoints had to be scoped to the requesting user rather than a shared service role, available only during execution, and respectful of that user’s access rights. A shared agent pool with static credentials failed all three.

Reading content that cannot be trusted. Agents here ingest complaints, email attachments, scanned PDFs, and images from outside the organization. The OWASP Top 10 for large language model (LLM) Applications (2025) names the threats that apply directly: prompt injection through ingested content (LLM01), sensitive information disclosure (LLM02), improper output handling (LLM05), and excessive agency (LLM06). Hidden instructions in an attached PDF are not hypothetical at this volume.

Embedding 2 billion documents without a quarter-long wait. Reliance hosts more than 2 billion documents, with individual tenants storing millions of Word files, PDFs, scanned forms, spreadsheets, images, and email. The team committed to onboarding even the largest tenant within a single working day. Because these documents inform regulatory decisions, quality could not be traded for throughput. A missed complaint erodes trust in the whole system.

Where the architecture landed

Holding four tensions at once narrowed the options considerably. Amazon Bedrock addressed them as one platform: multi-model access through a single API, the AWS Region residency and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) governance the AWS account already enforces, and Guardrails as production content controls rather than something to build.

The foundation resolves into three layers, shown in Figure 1. Data preparation embeds quality documents with Cohere Embed v4 on Amazon Bedrock and writes them to a per-tenant vector store on Amazon OpenSearch Service. Secure execution passes a user request through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which applies authentication and policy before handing it to an isolated microVM session that calls an Anthropic Claude model on Amazon Bedrock. Wrapping both, content protection applies Amazon Bedrock Guardrails twice: input filtering on the way in, output filtering before anything reaches the handler. Retrieval, execution, and screening stay in separate stages, so each can be enforced and evidenced on its own.

Choosing how to represent the data

Nothing else worked until the documents were retrievable. That meant accurately, across languages and formats, and not across a tenant boundary. The team evaluated embedding models against its own corpus rather than public leaderboards. The deciding questions were specific to this data: what a photo of a cracked housing has to do with the paragraph describing it, and a German complaint with an English CAPA.

Cohere Embed v4 on Amazon Bedrock won on five counts and they weren’t independent of each other. What was decided first was how much of the pipeline was made unnecessary. Quality records carry photos of defective products, scanned inspection forms, and annotated diagrams alongside text. Embed v4 places both modalities in one vector space. A photo of a cracked housing and the paragraph describing that defect are retrievable from a single query, with no separate pipeline per modality. Native multilingual support does the same work along the other axis: documents arrive in multiple languages, often inside one tenant’s corpus, and need no translation preprocessing. Two pipelines the team never had to build, and two fewer places for a document to fall out of retrieval.

The remaining three counts settled where the vectors could live and what they would cost. Customer data can’t leave its AWS Region, even for inference, so in-Region model availability on Amazon Bedrock was a precondition rather than a convenience. Embed v4 supports in-Region inference in the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1), Europe (Ireland) Region (eu-west-1), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo) Region (ap-northeast-1), covering three of Octave’s regional compliance requirements. Model and feature availability varies by Region and changes over time. For current coverage, see Regional availability by models in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. Within each Region, Amazon OpenSearch Service costs scale linearly with dimension count. That made Embed v4’s configurable output dimensions of 256–1,536 worth testing rather than accepting by default. Testing against representative production queries showed 512 dimensions holding target accuracy while cutting storage roughly 66 percent against the 1,536 default. The 128K token context window paid off elsewhere entirely: chunks of roughly 4K tokens pack many to a request, which is where the onboarding throughput came from.

Keeping tenants apart at runtime

The harder question was where to enforce tenant separation. Application code would have worked, but it would have meant every future feature team getting it right on every code path, where one missed check risks inadvertent cross-tenant disclosure. The team pushed isolation into the runtime instead. AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, enforces separation below the application layer, and because it stays framework- and model-independent, the agent framework and models chosen for the Complaint Triage Assistant were not constrained by the isolation decision.

Each user session runs in a dedicated microVM with its own CPU, memory, and filesystem, stopped and sanitized when the session ends. That is hardware-level separation designed to hold regardless of how the agent behaves. AgentCore carries the authenticated user’s identity through the whole execution chain: per-user OAuth token vaults verify the agent acts for that specific user rather than a shared service identity, and credentials are scoped per-agent and live only during the session. AgentCore Gateway authorizes at the tool, operation, and parameter level. Automated reasoning provides formal verification against the defined rules. It’s the same discipline behind IAM and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) policy validation. Figure 2 traces that separation across two tenants.

A complaint submitted by a quality handler at Tenant A therefore reaches only Tenant A’s token vault, tools, and sandbox in AgentCore Code Interpreter, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Tenant B’s session has no path to any of them.

Treating ingested content as untrusted

This tension had no clean answer. A complaint attachment is untrusted input, but it’s also the thing the agent exists to read, so suspicious content couldn’t be rejected. The team settled on defense in depth.

Octave applied Amazon Bedrock Guardrails over the agent logic rather than inside it, at three points in the complaint workflow. The ApplyGuardrail API evaluates text extracted from attachments before embedding, retrieved documents and tool outputs before they enter the agent’s context, and the synthesized brief before the handler sees it. Attachment-derived content is passed with input tagging, marking it as data rather than instruction. That is what makes an injection buried mid-document detectable. Personally Identifiable Information (PII) is masked on the way in.

Detection alone wasn’t sufficient, so bounded agency sits underneath. Whatever an agent is asked to do, AgentCore Gateway still governs which tools it can invoke, and document extraction runs in the AgentCore Code Interpreter sandbox with no network egress and no persistence beyond the session. A payload hidden in a PDF has to defeat every layer, not one.

The effect: detection and masking rates are tracked per tenant, so what the screening caught is something Octave can evidence rather than assert.

Getting 2 billion documents through the pipeline

Ahead of the embedding model sat the harder problem: extracting usable content from Word files, spreadsheets, digital PDFs, scanned pages, photographs, and email threads. Several languages appear, sometimes inside one record. And it had to run fast enough that onboarding took a day rather than a quarter. Figure 3 traces the resulting pipeline end to end.

Document events fan out through Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) and Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) into an AWS Step Functions state machine. That state machine orchestrates parsing, chunking, and embedding across concurrent AWS Lambda executions inside a dedicated Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC). Because parallelism comes from fanning batches across executions rather than scaling one resource, throughput grows without rearchitecting.

Parsing handles the heterogeneity: semantic hierarchy preserved from Word files and spreadsheets, optical character recognition (OCR) applied to scanned PDFs lacking a text layer, embedded images treated as first-class content. Chunks carry metadata: tenant, document type, source application, language, and a content hash. That metadata drives both retrieval filtering and per-tenant namespace enforcement.

The throughput came from packing. Interleaving many 4K chunks into single requests against Embed v4’s 128K context window cut the API calls for a large corpus by about an order of magnitude. In Octave’s internal testing on Amazon Bedrock, Embed v4 delivered 28 million tokens per minute. After tuning batch sizes with Cohere’s solutions architects until memory bottlenecks cleared, the pipeline sustained 1.4 million documents per 24 hours per tenant workload. That is what made the single-working-day commitment real.

The Complaint Triage Assistant

A hospital reports defective syringes to a medical device manufacturer, and the record lands with email, photos of damaged units, and supporting documentation attached. A quality handler has to piece the context together across those formats, work out whether anything like it has been reported before, and find what resolved it. Only then can a priority be assigned, often inside a reporting window measured in days.

The assistant is built with the Strands Agents SDK, open-sourced by AWS, which composes agentic workflows as graphs, with nodes as tool invocations or model calls and edges as the data dependencies between them. AgentCore runtime runs that graph and isolates it per session, and five stages carry a complaint from raw attachments to a finished brief.

Document extraction comes first. PDFs, images, email attachments, and videos all enter AgentCore Code Interpreter, which parses each artifact into a structured intermediate representation. A Claude model on Amazon Bedrock then summarizes the record, and that summary, rather than the raw multi-thousand-token source, becomes the retrieval query. Retrieval runs it against the tenant’s OpenSearch index of Embed v4 embeddings, surfacing similar past complaints and their CAPAs, with AgentCore Gateway enforcing that only authorized namespaces are reachable.

What comes back is not trusted on similarity alone. A separate model call scores results by confidence and discards matches that share vocabulary but differ in root cause. What survives goes to synthesis, where Anthropic Claude Sonnet on Amazon Bedrock assembles the output: key facts, sentiment, urgency indicators, the closest historical records with their outcomes, and a recommended triage priority.

Completed briefs are cached in Amazon DynamoDB with a per-environment time to live (TTL), so repeated views cost nothing extra. The handler no longer starts from zero, but from institutional memory.

Figure 4 places that engine behind a private API boundary. A portal request reaches AgentCore runtime through a private Amazon API Gateway and a Lambda function, and retrieval reads the document index through role-based access with pre-signed URLs while attachments stay in Amazon S3. Cached summaries and OpenTelemetry traces exit to the summarization table and the evaluation dashboard.

Figure 5 reduces the same path to a single line, with Guardrails filtering at both ends.

Proving what the agent did

Observability here is not only how the engineering team debugs but also how they integrate with system auditing capabilities to meet compliance requirements. An auditor can ask why a particular complaint was triaged the way it was, and “the model decided” will not survive that conversation.

AgentCore captures OpenTelemetry-compatible traces across every node of the graph: each model call, retrieval, and AgentCore Code Interpreter run. Months later, Octave can show which retrieved documents and prompts produced a given brief. The model invocation logging of Amazon Bedrock adds a per-tenant record of every request and response, scoped through the IAM identity AgentCore propagates, with costs attributing to the initiating tenant in Amazon CloudWatch.

Offline, AgentCore Evals reruns the workflow against expert-annotated ground truth after any change to prompts, models, or retrieval parameters, reporting summarization faithfulness, retrieval precision at K, and output completeness. A prompt that reads better but retrieves worse gets caught before users see it.

Results

The Complaint Triage Assistant has been running in production for three months, and the following numbers reflect that period.

The handler who used to open an investigation with nothing now opens it with the relevant history already assembled. The 4–6 hours Octave measures per investigation is the work the pipeline absorbed: extraction across formats, the hunt for precedent, and the reading it takes to tell a genuinely similar defect from a coincidence of wording.

The foundation also changed how quickly Octave ships. By its own accounting, development cycles for new AI capabilities went from months to weeks. Shared data preparation, secure execution, and retrieval are the three layers of Figure 1. They cut deployment time per use case by 50 percent, because each new capability inherits them rather than rebuilding them. That landed semantic search in Q2, two quarters ahead of the original Q4 target.

Looking back

The decision to build a foundation first was the one the team second-guessed most. Months of infrastructure work is hard to defend when stakeholders want an AI feature they can see. The next round of use cases has borne it out. Two choices carried it: isolation pushed into microVM sessions and identity propagation rather than application code, and embedding models evaluated against Octave’s own corpus, which surfaced the 512-dimension trade-off no benchmark would have shown.

The team also drew a line it chose not to cross. The assistant surfaces context and precedent. The quality handler still makes the call. In an industry where that call carries regulatory weight, that boundary shaped what got automated and what did not.

What’s next

Octave is now extending the foundation across the Reliance suite. Audit readiness monitoring, incident narrative generation, and predictive quality risk scoring are next, each building on the same infrastructure.

If your platform faces a similar tension: valuable data behind hard isolation requirements. Octave’s experience shows the trade-offs are workable. To learn more about the services behind this story, see Amazon Bedrock, the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation, and Cohere on Amazon Bedrock. For related architectural guidance, see AWS vector solutions: Build agentic AI where your data lives and Scaling agentic AI: Enterprise patterns without vendor lock-in.

entries.title: Access OpenAI GPT models on Amazon Bedrock from Canada with cross-Region inference
entries.summary: Canadian organizations can now access OpenAI GPT-5.6, GPT-6, and GPT-6.1 models on Amazon Bedrock from the Canada (Central) and Canada West (Calgary) Regions using cross-Region inference. This post covers the models and inference profiles, how to set up permissions, and how to invoke them with the Responses, Chat Completions, and Converse APIs.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Access OpenAI GPT models on Amazon Bedrock from Canada with cross-Region inference

Canadian organizations building generative AI applications on Amazon Bedrock often need the latest foundation models (FMs), such as OpenAI GPT-6.1, OpenAI GPT-6, and GPT-5.6, accessible from the Canadian AWS Regions. With Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference (CRIS), you can now access these models from Canada. OpenAI GPT-5.6 models (Sol, Terra, and Luna), GPT-6 (Astra, Sol, and Luna), and GPT-6.1 Sol are available from the Canada (Central) and Canada West (Calgary) Regions. Inference is processed in North America, with data-residency controls described later in this post.

Cross-Region inference is a capacity mechanism. Your application calls the Amazon Bedrock Runtime endpoint in your source Region. Amazon Bedrock then routes the request to a supported destination Region for processing. With this approach, you get access to a broader capacity pool that can help your application sustain throughput during demand spikes. You don’t need to manage destination Region routing in your application.

In this post, we walk through the GPT-5.6, GPT-6, and GPT-6.1 models available from Canada and the cross-Region inference profiles that serve them. We then show how to set up permissions and invoke the models with the OpenAI Responses API, Chat Completions API, and the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. For the Responses API, we include streaming and tool-use examples. Finally, we cover how to request quota increases, review the observability signals available in your source Region, and clean up when you are done.

Models available from Canada

With Amazon Bedrock, you can access three families of OpenAI models in Canada through cross-Region inference. The following table summarizes each model and its positioning.

ModelPositioning
GPT-6.1 SolStrong reasoning and coding for tasks where both performance and cost matter
GPT-6 AstraComplex end-to-end reasoning and agentic tasks
GPT-6 SolStrong reasoning and coding for recurring tasks with economics suited to regular use
GPT-6 LunaFast, low-cost inference for high-volume repeated tasks with adjustable reasoning effort per request
GPT-5.6 SolHigh reasoning, coding, and agentic workloads
GPT-5.6 TerraBalanced performance and cost for everyday production
GPT-5.6 LunaFast and affordable for high-volume, latency-sensitive applications

These models accept text and image inputs, return text, and support a 1-million-token context window, reasoning mode, and tool calling. GPT-6.1 Sol supports the same context window and tool calling, with additional input and output modalities documented in its model card. GPT-5.6, GPT-6, and GPT-6.1 also support prompt caching on Amazon Bedrock (see the Prompt caching section). These models are available through the OpenAI Responses API, the OpenAI Chat Completions API, and the Amazon Bedrock Converse API on the 

bedrock-runtime
endpoint.

For pricing, see Amazon Bedrock pricing. For per-model Region availability, see the model cards in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide.

Cross-Region inference profiles from Canada

Amazon Bedrock inference profiles are logical identifiers you pass in place of a raw model ID. Each profile defines a model and the set of Regions to which Amazon Bedrock can route a request. Two profile types are available from Canada:

  • US geographic (prefixed 
    us.
    ) routes requests to your Canadian source Region and US Regions. Choose this profile when your workload requires inference processing to remain within North America (Canada and the US).
  • Global (prefixed 
    global.
    ) routes requests to supported commercial AWS Regions where the model is deployed. This draws on a broader capacity pool at the time of the request.

Endpoint availability differs by model and source Region, as shown in the following table.

ModelUS geographic profileGlobal profile
GPT-6.1 Solca-central-1, ca-west-1ca-central-1, ca-west-1
GPT-6 Astra / Sol / Lunaca-central-1, ca-west-1ca-central-1, ca-west-1
GPT-5.6 Sol / Terra / Lunaca-central-1, ca-west-1ca-central-1

Profile membership and model availability can change. The global profile for the GPT-5.6 models is available only from 

ca-central-1
. From 
ca-west-1
, use the US geographic profile for GPT-5.6. Verify the active profiles for your source Region before deployment, either with the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) or on the console (see the following section), or see the Cross-Region inference support documentation.

Getting started

The following sections walk through the setup and code needed to invoke these models from your Canadian source Region.

Prerequisites

Before you begin, confirm that you have the following:

  • An AWS account with the Canada (Central) 
    ca-central-1
    or Canada West (Calgary) 
    ca-west-1
    Region enabled as your source Region.
  • An AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role or user with permissions to invoke the inference profiles (see Set up permissions).
  • A service control policy (SCP) that allows the inference profiles in your source Region, if your organization enforces SCPs (see SCP considerations).
  • Python 3.9 or later with the 
    openai
    , 
    boto3
    , and 
    aws-bedrock-token-generator
    packages installed.

Set up permissions

For quick exploration, attach the AWS managed policy 

AmazonBedrockLimitedAccess
. For deployed workloads with stricter access controls, use a least-privilege custom policy. The following example grants access to the GPT-6 Astra global profile from 
ca-central-1
:

If you authenticate through the API-key path (bearer token for the OpenAI SDK), also grant 

bedrock:CallWithBearerToken
. For the Responses API, add 
bedrock:InvokeModel
on 
arn:aws:bedrock:ca-central-1:*:project/default
.

SCP considerations

If your organization restricts Regions through SCPs, use the 

bedrock:InferenceProfileArn
condition key to allow CRIS traffic while blocking direct calls to unapproved Regions. The following SCP denies Amazon Bedrock inference outside your approved source Regions unless the request uses a CRIS inference profile:

With this condition, Amazon Bedrock can route to the profile’s destination Regions even when those Regions are otherwise denied by your SCP. Every destination Region in your chosen profile must be allowed for the request to succeed. For more detail, see Set up cross-Region inference in multi-account environments.

Verify active inference profiles

Before invoking a model, you can verify which profiles are active in your source Region with the AWS CLI. The following command lists the active OpenAI profiles from 

ca-central-1
. To run the same check from Calgary, replace 
ca-central-1
with 
ca-west-1
.

The Amazon Bedrock console offers the same view. Open the console, choose Canada (Central) or Canada West (Calgary) as your Region, choose Cross-Region inference under Inference, and review the available profiles.

The following screenshot shows the active OpenAI inference profiles listed on the Amazon Bedrock console for the Canada (Central) Region.

Invoke the models through Amazon Bedrock Runtime

GPT-5.6, GPT-6, and GPT-6.1 support three access paths on the 

bedrock-runtime
endpoint: the OpenAI Responses API, the OpenAI Chat Completions API, and the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. The OpenAI-compatible APIs are called on the 
/openai/v1
paths of the endpoint. The endpoint accepts either AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) or an Amazon Bedrock API key.

The following examples use the Amazon Bedrock token generator for Python to create a short-term Amazon Bedrock API key from your current AWS credentials, so your application does not need to store a static key.

OpenAI Responses API

For applications that already use the OpenAI SDK with the Responses API, point the client at the Regional Amazon Bedrock Runtime endpoint and pass the inference profile ID as the model.

For streaming output, set 

stream=True
and iterate over the response events, printing text as it arrives:

OpenAI Chat Completions API

The OpenAI Chat Completions format works through the same endpoint.

For the full list of supported parameters, including reasoning effort levels, see the model cards in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide.

Amazon Bedrock Converse API

Use the Converse API when your application calls Amazon Bedrock through an AWS SDK. Boto3 resolves credentials through the standard AWS credential chain.

The same call works for GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, and GPT-6.1 Sol by changing the inference profile ID. The following example uses the US geographic profile for GPT-6 Sol and the global profile for GPT-6 Luna. Both were validated from 

ca-central-1
.

Tool use

These models support client-side tool use (function calling). Define tools in the 

tools
parameter, and the model returns a structured tool-call request for your application to execute.

Prompt caching

GPT-5.6, GPT-6, and GPT-6.1 support prompt caching on Amazon Bedrock to reduce the cost and latency of repeated prompt prefixes. Implicit caching requires no changes to your code: Amazon Bedrock automatically caches eligible prefixes of 1,024 tokens or more. Cached tokens read on subsequent requests are billed at a discounted rate and do not count against your tokens-per-minute quota. Cached tokens appear in the response usage object and in Amazon CloudWatch metrics so you can track usage. For cache-write pricing, minimum prefix sizes, and support for explicit cache breakpoints, see the prompt caching documentation and the individual model cards.

Quota management

Cross-Region inference quotas on the 

bedrock-runtime
endpoint are measured in tokens per minute (TPM) per model. Each quota combines input and output tokens against a single limit. US geographic and global inference profiles have separate quota allocations, so switching between them changes the pool you draw from.

Token consumption combines input tokens, cache-write input tokens, and output tokens. Output tokens are multiplied by the model’s burndown rate, so output-heavy workloads consume quota faster than raw token counts suggest. Before a production rollout, request quota increases early and monitor quota utilization. Test with representative prompts, output lengths, streaming behavior, concurrency, and peak traffic.

To request a quota increase, follow these steps:

  • Open the Service Quotas console in 
    ca-central-1
    or 
    ca-west-1
    .
  • Choose Amazon Bedrock, then select the quota named “Cross-Region InvokeModel tokens per minute” for the model that you need.
  • Choose Request increase at account level, enter your target value, and submit the request.

For details on how token usage and costs are tracked, see Track usage and costs in Amazon Bedrock.

Observability

Because these models run through the Amazon Bedrock Runtime API, requests made through an inference profile appear in your observability tooling the same way on-demand requests do. Invocation logs and Amazon CloudWatch metrics are recorded in your source Region. This holds regardless of where the request was processed. Your observability stays in one place.

  • AWS CloudTrail logs every request, recording which destination Region served it in the 
    additionalEventData.inferenceRegion
    field. For example:
  • Amazon CloudWatch metrics are published per inference profile, covering invocation count, token count, latency, throttles, and errors.
  • Model invocation logging delivers full request and response payloads to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon CloudWatch Logs. To activate it on the Amazon Bedrock console, choose Settings, then choose Model invocation logging. You can also call the 
    PutModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration
    API. It is off by default.
  • AWS Data Exports itemizes spend by model and profile.

Amazon CloudWatch Coding Agent Insights

If you use these models to power AI coding assistants such as OpenAI Codex, Amazon CloudWatch Coding Agent Insights provides a dedicated dashboard. It surfaces token usage, API request counts, active users, and cost attribution across dimensions such as department, team, and environment. To activate it, configure your coding agent to export telemetry to Amazon CloudWatch. For the setup steps, see Set up OpenTelemetry for OpenAI Codex.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges after testing, remove the resources you created:

  • Turn off model invocation logging. On the Amazon Bedrock console, choose Settings, then choose Model invocation logging, or call 
    DeleteModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration
    . This stops delivery of logs to Amazon S3 and Amazon CloudWatch Logs.
  • Delete or detach the IAM policies and any Amazon Bedrock API keys that you created for testing.

The inference profiles themselves are system-defined and incur no cost when they aren’t in use.

Security and compliance

Cross-Region inference is designed to protect your data in transit and at rest. Requests travel over the AWS private backbone encrypted with TLS 1.2+ rather than the public internet. For Canadian customers, your data at rest stays in your source Region by default. This includes invocation logs, knowledge bases, and configurations. Only the transient inference computation happens in the destination Region, and by default model providers don’t have access to your prompts or completions.

There’s one consideration specific to OpenAI models. Content flagged by automated abuse classifiers might be retained for up to 30 days in the destination Region for review. If you want to constrain processing to North America (Canada and the US), you can choose the US geographic profile. We recommend reviewing Amazon Bedrock abuse detection with your compliance team.

For a more detailed look at Canadian data residency patterns, see Cross-Region Inference and Canadian Data Residency: A Technical Architecture Guide.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how to access OpenAI GPT-5.6 (Sol, Terra, and Luna), GPT-6 (Astra, Sol, and Luna), and GPT-6.1 Sol from Canada. These models are available from the Canada (Central) and Canada West (Calgary) Regions using cross-Region inference on Amazon Bedrock. We covered the available inference profiles, how to set up permissions and an example SCP, and how to invoke the models with the Responses, Chat Completions, and Converse APIs. For the Responses API, we included streaming and tool-use examples. We also showed how to request quota increases, review usage, and clean up your test resources.

To get started, review the OpenAI model cards in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide, then open the Amazon Bedrock console and send a test prompt through an inference profile. For pricing, see the Amazon Bedrock pricing page.

If you have questions or feedback, leave a comment on this post.

entries.title: Discover tools at runtime with AWS Agent Registry
entries.summary: Hardcoded tool wiring breaks down as an agent's catalog grows from a handful of tools to hundreds. This post walks through a runtime Discover, Instantiate, Execute loop built on AWS Agent Registry, where an orchestrator discovers MCP servers and A2A agents through semantic search at runtime instead of compiling every tool at build time.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Discover tools at runtime with AWS Agent Registry

Runtime discovery with AWS Agent Registry can help address a problem that agent demos might hide. Hardcoded tools work fine for a handful, start to degrade at a few dozen, and become unmanageable beyond that. Enterprise systems expose hundreds of internal APIs for pricing, support, orders, inventory, and customer data. In these systems, the model can spend more tokens disambiguating tool names than reasoning about the user’s request. Each new capability requires a code change in the orchestrator, a redeploy, and a coordinated release across teams that would much rather ship on their own cadence.

This pattern can arise across enterprise software as a service (SaaS) engagements where teams expose large internal API surfaces to agentic consumers. Build-time wiring can become a bottleneck as the catalog expands. One approach is to change how the orchestrator accesses its tools: instead of compiling every tool into the agent, the agent can discover relevant tools at runtime.

AWS Agent Registry is a managed service for cataloging and discovering Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, agents, and agent skills. Publishers register protocol-specific descriptors and searchable descriptions. At runtime, an orchestrator can search approved, discoverable records and use the returned endpoint and descriptor content to construct a client. Registry search results do not return the capability’s invocation credentials or authentication scheme.

This post walks through the Discover → Instantiate → Execute loop demonstrated by the refactored Python sample. The code deploys an order-management MCP server through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, two agent-to-agent (A2A) agents on AgentCore runtime, a Registry, and an orchestrator. The sample directory contains the deployment script, orchestrator, helper modules, and cleanup script.

Solution overview: discover, instantiate, execute

The orchestrator agent in this sample has no built-in knowledge of tools or agents.

Discover

The orchestrator sends a natural-language query to the AWS Agent Registry data plane. The search response includes record identity, name, description, record type, status, version, and protocol descriptors such as MCP server metadata or an A2A agent card. It does not include invocation credentials. The application must obtain and apply the appropriate credentials through a separate, trusted configuration path.

Instantiate

For each returned record, the orchestrator constructs a client from the descriptor type. In this sample, the registered MCP server represents tools that were first added as targets to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. The MCP descriptor therefore points to the Gateway endpoint. The orchestrator fetches a Cognito OAuth access token separately and uses it when creating the 

MCPClient
. A2A records contain an agent card whose URL identifies an AgentCore runtime endpoint. The wrapper invokes that runtime through the boto3 data-plane client, which signs the request with the caller’s AWS credentials. Registry discovery supplies connection metadata, not the authentication material.

Execute

An ephemeral inner agent is built with only the dynamically-discovered tools. The large language model (LLM) picks the right one(s) for the request, and the result is synthesized back to the user. After the turn finishes, the inner agent and its clients are torn down. The next request gets a fresh search and a fresh tool set.

The reference architecture used in the sample includes AWS Agent Registry, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Cognito, AWS Lambda, and AWS Secrets Manager.

  • AWS Agent Registry provides the governed, searchable catalog queried by the orchestrator. Only records that complete the configured approval workflow are available through the discoverable data plane.
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway exposes the order-management Lambda tools as an MCP server. The sample configures Cognito JWT authorization for inbound Gateway calls and uses the Gateway AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role to invoke the Lambda target.
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime hosts the orchestrator and the Pricing and Customer Support A2A agents. Runtime invocations use IAM-authorized Boto3 calls.
  • Amazon Bedrock provides the foundation model (FM) used by the orchestrator and A2A agents. The sample currently configures an Anthropic Claude Sonnet model through a cross-Region model ID. See Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.

Three demo scenarios exercise the discovery loop with different capability combinations. The first is an MCP-only call (order status). The second chains MCP + A2A (pricing and discounts). The third tests a pure semantic match against ambiguous user intent: return and refund, where those words don’t appear in the matched A2A agent’s name.

Technical implementation

The linked runtime-discovery sample deploys the dependencies, creates and populates the Registry, verifies discovery, deploys the orchestrator, and runs three demos. orchestrator_agent.py contains the per-request discovery loop. utils.py parses Registry descriptors and creates MCP and A2A clients. cleanup.py removes resources.

1. The registration model

A Registry record contains a searchable description plus a protocol-specific descriptor. The sample uses the Agent Registry control-plane client for Registry and record lifecycle operations and the Agent Registry data-plane client for runtime discovery.

Creating a Registry with manual approval and IAM authorization.

The 

recordType
field is required when creating a record. In this sample, MCP servers use 
recordType="MCP"
and A2A-backed agents use 
recordType="AGENT"
. Protocol metadata is stored under 
mcpServer
or 
a2aAgentCard
in the 
descriptors
object. An MCP descriptor contains server metadata and tool definitions. An A2A descriptor contains the agent card. The descriptors contain connection metadata but not the credentials that a consumer must present when invoking the capability.

Building current public-SDK descriptor shapes for MCP and A2A records.

Write descriptions in user-facing language that distinguishes the capability from neighboring records. Descriptor content supplies the protocol-specific server, tool, or agent-card data. Search quality should be evaluated with representative queries. This post does not assume that catalog growth automatically improves ranking.

Creating a Registry record with the current control-plane shape.

2. Approval workflow

With 

autoApproval
set to false, a new record must move from 
DRAFT
to 
PENDING_APPROVAL
and then 
APPROVED
. The submit and status-update actions are IAM-authorized, allowing publisher and approver permissions to be separated. Only approved records are returned by the discoverable Registry data plane.

The two-step approval transition.

3. The discovery layer

The data-plane client supports hybrid keyword and semantic search across discoverable records. The latest method name is search_discoverable_registry_records. Results expose normalized record fields and discoverable descriptors. They don’t expose the capability’s invocation credentials.

Searching approved, discoverable records across protocols.

In the sample scenario, a return-and-refund query retrieves the Customer Support Agent because its description captures that intent. Treat this as a demo result, not a general claim that ranking improves merely because the catalog is larger.

4. The orchestrator

The orchestrator is a Strands agent deployed to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime. It exposes 

discover_and_execute
, which searches the Registry, parses each returned descriptor, creates the corresponding MCP or A2A client, and builds a request-scoped inner agent from only those discovered capabilities.

The core of 

discover_and_execute
fits in a single code block:

The orchestrator’s discover/instantiate/execute loop.

The sample fans out several search queries to improve recall for its order-management domain, deduplicates records, and tears down MCP clients after the request. That fan-out is a sample-specific orchestration choice, not a Registry requirement. Authentication remains outside discovery: the Gateway OAuth token is obtained from Cognito configuration and Secrets Manager, whereas A2A runtime calls are signed through the boto3 session.

5. Running the three demos

Each demo exercises a different shape of the discovery loop.

Demo 1: Order status (MCP only)

A request that resolves to a single MCP tool call.

The Registry returns the order management MCP server. The orchestrator calls 

get_order_status
through Gateway, the LLM synthesizes a human-readable response, and the inner agent terminates. No A2A involvement on this turn.

Demo 2: Pricing and discounts (MCP + A2A)

A request that resolves to a multi-protocol chain.

The Registry returns the order management MCP server and the pricing A2A agent: two protocols, one natural-language query. The LLM calls 

get_order_status
to fetch line items, then calls the pricing agent on runtime for discount analysis, then synthesizes a single recommendation.

Demo 3: Return and refund (semantic match)

A request whose intent is not literally present in any tool name.

This demo shows the value of semantic discovery. The phrase ‘return refund’ doesn’t appear in the Customer Support Agent’s registered name. The hybrid search ranks it highly because its description captures the intent. Without Registry, the orchestrator would need hardcoded knowledge of which agent handles returns.

6. Observability

Instrument the discovery and invocation path using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability and Amazon CloudWatch where appropriate. Useful signals include Registry search success and failure, selected record identifiers, client-construction errors, downstream invocation outcomes, end-to-end trace correlation, and application errors. The sample grants Amazon CloudWatch Logs permissions, but it doesn’t create custom metrics or dashboards. Production teams should define the traces, logs, and alerts required for their operating model. Production deployments should also apply Amazon Bedrock Guardrails as a standard control on agent responses.

What teams gain from governed runtime discovery

After the discovery loop is in place, several capabilities that were previously coupled to orchestrator releases become independent.

  • Decoupled publishing. Teams can deploy and register their own MCP servers, agents, and skills. Approval policy determines when a published record becomes available to consumers.
  • No orchestrator code change for newly approved records. In this pattern, adding a compatible, approved Registry record doesn’t require adding a tool-specific import or endpoint to the orchestrator. Changes to protocols, authentication setup, or orchestration policy can still require code or configuration updates.
  • Governed discovery. With manual approval, only reviewed and approved records become discoverable. IAM permissions can separate record publishers from approvers.
  • Separated authentication. Registry authorization can use IAM or custom JWT. Capability invocation authentication is separate: the sample uses Cognito OAuth for Gateway and Boto3/IAM signing for AgentCore runtime. Search results don’t return those credentials.
  • Catalog search instead of prompt stuffing. With hybrid Registry search, the orchestrator retrieves a small candidate set instead of placing the full catalog in the model context. Search quality depends on descriptions, descriptor quality, query design, and evaluation.

When not to use runtime discovery

Runtime discovery is not necessary for every workload. Two patterns can still favor explicit build-time wiring:

  • Small, stable catalogs. If the complete capability set is small and changes rarely, explicit build-time wiring might be simpler and avoid an additional discovery request.
  • Fixed pipelines. When the same capabilities always run in a fixed order, implementing them as a deterministic flow is more straightforward and keeps tracing focused.

Conclusion

Discovery of assets from Registry at runtime makes the orchestrator less dependent on a fixed catalog. Against an AWS Agent Registry, it can search approved capabilities with hybrid semantic and keyword search, parse MCP or A2A descriptors, and instantiate request-scoped clients. Governance determines what is discoverable. Authentication remains an explicit concern for the Registry and each invoked capability.

AWS Agent Registry is generally available with capabilities that extend beyond this single-account sample:

  • Organization-wide discovery and cross-account sharing can expose governed records across account boundaries through supported AWS Organizations and sharing mechanisms.
  • Automatic capability synchronization can populate supported descriptors from a URL. Credential-provider configuration on that synchronization request is used to fetch descriptor content. It isn’t returned to runtime consumers as invocation authentication.
  • Approval workflows can use Registry status APIs and IAM permissions to connect CI checks, security review, or human approval to the 
    DRAFT
    → 
    PENDING_APPROVAL
    → 
    APPROVED
    lifecycle.
  • Tagging, AWS CloudFormation support, and infrastructure-as-code patterns can make Registry deployment and governance repeatable. Evaluation should verify search relevance and invocation behavior for the organization’s own catalog.

Run the runtime-discovery sample, then register one compatible MCP server or agent of your own. Confirm that its descriptor, approval state, authentication path, and search behavior match your production requirements.

Learn more

  • AWS Agent Registry general availability announcement
  • AWS Agent Registry documentation
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore console (Registry)
  • AWS Agent Registry general availability technical blog post

entries.title: Securing AI agent identity with X.509 PKI on AWS
entries.summary: Learn how to secure multi-agent AI systems with cryptographic identity using Keyfactor EJBCA and AWS services. This reference architecture combines signed request envelopes, user-signed delegation assertions, RFC 8693 audience-scoped tokens, and real-time OCSP revocation to prove agent identity and prevent request forgery across agent-to-agent and MCP tool calls.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Securing AI agent identity with X.509 PKI on AWS

When AI agents access databases, APIs, and sensitive business operations, establishing cryptographic identity through X.509 public key infrastructure (PKI) becomes a critical requirement. The core challenge is proving which agent made a request, preventing forgery between agents, and confirming that each agent acts only on behalf of an authorized user. Traditional approaches such as sharing API keys between components or passing OAuth tokens through agent chains fall short of the zero-trust requirements that enterprise deployments demand.

Multi-agent AI frameworks increasingly use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect agents to external tools and data sources. MCP defines how a large language model (LLM)-powered agent invokes tools such as database queries or email operations. However, MCP has no built-in authentication standard. It is transport-agnostic by design. This creates a critical gap: Without proper identity mechanisms, any component could impersonate an agent, replay intercepted credentials, or invoke tools without authorization.

In this post, we show you how to address this gap using Keyfactor EJBCA combined with AWS services. EJBCA is a PKI platform that supports high-availability deployment, REST API automation, and Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) validation. The reference architecture uses four complementary security mechanisms. First, signed request envelopes provide cryptographic proof-of-possession on every agent call. Second, user-signed delegation assertions authorize agents without sharing credentials. Third, RFC 8693 audience-scoped tokens limit the scope of exposure from any single token disclosure. Fourth, real-time OCSP revocation checking propagates credential changes immediately across all agents.

The solution uses Amazon Bedrock for LLM inference through the AWS Strands Agents SDK. While this reference architecture uses a database as the protected resource, the same authentication pattern applies to any MCP-compatible tool server. Complete source code for all examples is available in the accompanying GitHub repository.

About Keyfactor EJBCA

Keyfactor provides a widely adopted machine identity management platform used by more than 1,500 enterprise customers worldwide, according to Keyfactor. These organizations span financial services, healthcare, manufacturing, and government. Keyfactor helps organizations establish and maintain cryptographic trust through certificate lifecycle management, PKI operations, and machine identity governance.

EJBCA Enterprise is Keyfactor’s Certificate Authority (CA) and PKI platform, designed for high-availability deployment and REST API automation. Available as an enterprise product, EJBCA provides X.509 certificate issuance, OCSP validation, certificate revocation list (CRL) distribution, and full certificate lifecycle management through both a web console and REST API. EJBCA supports deployment on-premises, in containers, or on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2).

The partnership between AWS and Keyfactor brings together AWS managed services (Amazon Bedrock, AWS Secrets Manager, Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS)) with PKI infrastructure that supports certificate lifecycle management, automated enrollment, and real-time revocation. This combination addresses a gap in the AI agent ecosystem. While AWS provides the compute, storage, and AI inference layers, Keyfactor provides the cryptographic identity layer that binds agents to verifiable, revocable, short-lived credentials. This joint reference architecture, developed collaboratively by the AWS and Keyfactor engineering teams, demonstrates how to integrate these technologies. You can adapt the patterns shown here to your own multi-agent deployments.

Solution overview

The architecture implements three authentication layers, each addressing a different trust boundary in the agent communication chain. These three layers use the four security mechanisms introduced earlier: signed envelopes for proof-of-possession, delegation assertions for credential-free authorization, audience-scoped tokens for exposure limitation, and OCSP for real-time revocation. The mechanisms combine across layers as shown in the following table.

LayerTrust boundaryMechanismValidates
1. User AuthUser to SystemOAuth + X.509 cert + delegation mintingUser identity, credential binding
2. Agent-to-AgentAgent to AgentSigned envelopes (PoP + nonce + timestamp)Caller identity, request freshness, no replay
3. MCP AuthAgent to Tool ServerScoped token + envelope + delegationAll identities, authorization chain, OCSP

Figure 1 shows the three authentication layers and how credentials flow between the user, agents, and the MCP tool server. The diagram illustrates the separation between user credentials (which stay in the login flow), agent credentials (scoped per agent), and the delegation chain that connects them.

Figure 2 illustrates the detailed traffic flow during a typical user session. It shows the sequence of authentication steps from login through certificate issuance, agent delegation, tool invocation, and session cleanup.

AWS services used

The following AWS services form the foundation of the reference architecture.

ServicePurpose
Amazon BedrockLLM inference through Strands Agents SDK
Amazon RDS for MySQLApplication database accessed through MCP tools
Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES)Email delivery for the Email Agent
AWS Secrets ManagerSecure storage for PKCS12 bundles, tokens, and metadata
Amazon EC2Hosts Keycloak IDP and EJBCA PKI server

Solution walkthrough

The following steps walk through each component of the architecture, from initial user login through to session cleanup. Each step builds on the previous one, establishing a chain of trust that connects the human user to the final tool execution.

Prerequisites

  • An active AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock, Amazon RDS for MySQL, Amazon SES, and AWS Secrets Manager.
  • Keycloak 26.2 or later (required for RFC 8693 standard token exchange. Previous versions use a legacy exchange that is incompatible).
  • Keyfactor EJBCA Enterprise with REST API V1 and an OCSP responder configured.
  • EJBCA API administrator certificate (
    api-admin.p12
    ) for REST API authentication.
  • Python 3.9+ development environment.
  • Familiarity with X.509 certificates, OCSP, OAuth 2.0, RSA digital signatures, and PKCS#12 key stores.

Step 1: User login, certificate issuance, and delegation minting

The login flow establishes the user’s identity through three mechanisms and then delegates authority to the AI agents without sharing the user’s credentials. This separation is critical: Agents receive proof of authorization without ever holding the user’s private key or full-session OAuth token.

First, the application authenticates the user against Keycloak using an OAuth 2.0 password grant, receiving a full-session access token and refresh token. Immediately after, the application performs an RFC 8693 token exchange to obtain a downscoped token. This token’s audience is restricted to the MCP server. Only this limited token is handed to agents. If it’s inadvertently exposed, it can’t access any other service in the organization.

Second, the application generates an RSA 2048+ key pair locally and submits a Certificate Signing Request (CSR) to EJBCA through the 

pkcs10enroll
REST API endpoint. EJBCA signs the CSR and returns the certificate. The application bundles the certificate and private key into a PKCS12 container and stores it in AWS Secrets Manager. The private key never leaves the application boundary. It is not sent to EJBCA, not shared with agents, and not stored on the filesystem. Three agent certificates are issued using the same CSR-based flow, one per agent role.

Third, the user’s private key signs a delegation assertion. This is a JSON document listing the SHA-256 fingerprints of all three agent certificates, along with the user’s subject name, issuance time, and expiry. This delegation proves that the user authorized these specific agents to act on their behalf. Agents carry this delegation instead of the user’s certificate.

Step 2: Agent-to-agent signed envelopes

When the orchestrator agent routes a request to a sub-agent (such as the MySQL agent or Email agent), it does not simply pass its certificate for identification. Instead, it signs the entire request payload, including the tool name, arguments, a timestamp, and a cryptographically random nonce, using its private key with 

RSA-PSS-SHA256
. The resulting signed envelope provides proof-of-possession. The receiving agent can verify that the caller actually holds the private key corresponding to the presented certificate.

The receiving agent performs six validation checks on the envelope before processing the request:

  • Signature verification: Proves the sender possesses the private key (proof-of-possession).
  • Timestamp freshness: The envelope must be within 
    ENVELOPE_MAX_AGE_SECONDS
    (default 60 seconds) of the current time.
  • Nonce uniqueness: The 
    ReplayCache
    rejects any previously seen nonce, preventing request replay.
  • CA chain validation: The sender’s certificate must chain to the trusted CA (
    UserCA.pem
    ).
  • Role authorization: The certificate CN’s role suffix must be in 
    ALLOWED_CALLER_ROLES
    for this agent.
  • OCSP revocation check: A real-time check against EJBCA confirms the certificate has not been revoked.

If the orchestrator needs to re-send the same prompt (for example, after a transient failure), it must create a new envelope with a fresh nonce. Old envelopes can’t be replayed, even by the legitimate sender.

Step 3: MCP server authentication

The MCP server (FastMCP) is the final trust boundary before any database operation runs. It performs four validation checks on every tool invocation, implementing defense-in-depth. Even if one credential is subject to unauthorized access, the remaining checks prevent unauthorized operations.

The authentication sequence:

  • Token introspection: A POST to the Keycloak 
    /token/introspect
    endpoint verifies the token is active and its audience contains “mcp-server”. A full-session token without the correct audience is rejected.
  • Envelope verification: The agent’s signed envelope is validated for signature correctness, timestamp freshness, nonce uniqueness, CA chain trust, role match (
    mysql-agent
    ), and OCSP non-revocation.
  • Delegation verification: The user’s delegation assertion is validated. The signature proves the user’s key holder authorized this delegation, the calling agent’s certificate fingerprint appears in the authorized list, and the user’s certificate is checked through OCSP.
  • Identity cross-check: The token username, the delegation subject, and the agent certificate CN prefix must all match. This confirms a single consistent identity chain from user through to tool execution.

Step 4: Replay prevention

Every signed envelope carries a unique nonce, a 128-bit cryptographically random hex string generated with Python’s secrets module. The 

ReplayCache
is a thread-safe in-memory store that remembers every nonce until its freshness window expires (2x 
ENVELOPE_MAX_AGE_SECONDS
). If the same nonce appears in a second request, the envelope is immediately rejected, even if its signature is valid and the timestamp is fresh.

The timestamp validation complements the nonce check. An envelope’s timestamp must be within 

ENVELOPE_MAX_AGE_SECONDS
(default 60 seconds) of the server’s current time. Together, these mechanisms address four unauthorized access scenarios:
  • Recorded replay: An unauthorized user captures a valid envelope and resubmits it later. The nonce was already seen.
  • Delayed delivery: An envelope intercepted in transit arrives after the freshness window. The timestamp check fails.
  • Stale request reuse: An old envelope cached by a proxy is resubmitted. Both nonce and timestamp checks fail.
  • Precomputed forgery: An unauthorized user cannot predict future nonces to pre-sign envelopes.

Step 5: Client-side key generation

A critical security property of this architecture is that private keys are generated locally and never transmitted to any external system. The application generates RSA 2048+ key pairs using the Python cryptography library. It constructs a CSR containing only the public key and subject information, and sends only the CSR to EJBCA through the 

pkcs10enroll
endpoint.

EJBCA validates the CSR, applies the certificate profile (7-day validity, key usage constraints), signs it with the CA key, and returns the issued certificate. The application then bundles the locally held private key with the returned certificate into a PKCS12 container and stores it in AWS Secrets Manager.

This design provides several security properties:

  • The user’s private key is used only at login to sign the delegation assertion. It’s never shared with agents.
  • Each agent’s private key is used only by that agent to sign envelopes. It’s never shared between agents.
  • EJBCA never sees or stores private keys. It operates purely as a certificate authority.
  • If Secrets Manager is subject to unauthorized access, the PKCS12 password (stored separately) adds an additional layer.
  • Key material can be rotated independently by re-enrolling with a new CSR at next login.

Step 6: Complete logout and credential revocation

Logout triggers a revocation cascade that immediately invalidates all outstanding credentials. The sequence results in no remaining valid credentials after completion:

  • Revoke user certificate in EJBCA: This immediately invalidates all outstanding delegations, because delegation verification checks the user’s certificate through OCSP in real time.
  • Revoke all three agent certificates: This invalidates all outstanding signed envelopes, since envelope verification includes OCSP.
  • Delete all secrets from AWS Secrets Manager: Using 
    ForceDeleteWithoutRecovery
    for immediate removal with no recovery window.
  • Terminate Keycloak session: Invalidates the downscoped token through the session termination endpoint.

The revocation cascade is the key security property. Revoking a single user certificate at the PKI layer promptly revokes all downstream agent authority without needing to individually revoke tokens, delete sessions, or contact each agent. OCSP provides the propagation mechanism, and because every request checks OCSP, the effect is immediate.

Security considerations

The design choices in this architecture address several security properties that are important for production multi-agent deployments.

Private key isolation. The user’s private key exists only during the login flow and is used solely to sign the delegation. Agent keys are scoped per-agent and never shared. No key material crosses trust boundaries.

Delegation compared to credential sharing. Agents prove their authority through a cryptographic chain (delegation to agent fingerprint to envelope signature) without ever holding user credentials. If an agent key is exposed, only that agent’s key is revealed, not the user’s.

Audience-scoped tokens. RFC 8693 token exchange produces a token accepted only by the MCP server. An inadvertently disclosed downscoped token cannot authenticate against Keycloak admin APIs, other services, or even a different MCP server instance.

Replay prevention. The combination of per-request nonces and a 60-second freshness window confirms that every request is single-use and time-bound. The 

ReplayCache
is thread-safe and self-cleaning.

Fail-closed design. Every validation failure results in immediate denial. OCSP unreachable: deny. Invalid signature: deny. Expired timestamp: deny. Replayed nonce: deny. Wrong audience: deny. There’s no graceful degradation for security checks.

Revocation cascade. Revoking one user certificate promptly invalidates all delegations, all agent authority, and all outstanding envelopes. This is propagated through real-time OCSP without requiring individual credential cleanup.

Forward-only trust chain. The 

ALLOWED_CALLER_ROLES
map enforces that only 
orchestrator-agent
can call 
mysql-agent
and 
email-agent
. Sub-agents cannot call each other, can’t call upward to the orchestrator, and cannot impersonate the user.

AI governance considerations

The PKI architecture provides built-in behavior boundaries for the AI agents in this system. Production deployments should use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to enforce content filtering, topic avoidance, and grounding checks on agent responses, alongside the PKI-based access controls described in this post.

  • Tool boundaries: The AI agent operates under strict tool constraints. It can only invoke pre-defined MCP tools (
    execute_sql
    , 
    describe_table
    , 
    list_tables
    ). The agent can’t execute arbitrary code or access resources outside its certificate scope.
  • Human oversight: All agent actions are logged and auditable. AWS CloudTrail captures AWS API calls, and the MCP server logs every validated tool invocation with the full identity chain (user, agent, timestamp, and operation).
  • Data handling: User queries and results stay within the authenticated session boundary. The audience-scoped token confines data access to the specific MCP server instance.
  • Certificate-based behavior boundaries: Agents can only invoke tools they hold valid certificates for. An agent without a 
    mysql-agent
    certificate cannot access the database, regardless of what the LLM might generate as instructions.

Extending the architecture

You can extend this architecture to support additional agent types, horizontal scaling, and multi-tenant isolation. The following paragraphs describe the most common extension points.

  • To add new agent types, you only need to add an entry in 
    ALLOWED_CALLER_ROLES
    . Certificates are automatically issued at login, and the delegation assertion dynamically includes the new agent’s fingerprint. No infrastructure changes are required.
  • For horizontal scaling, you can deploy EJBCA’s OCSP responder in high-availability mode behind a load balancer. AWS Secrets Manager supports high request rates suitable for this workload. The 
    ReplayCache
    can be backed by Amazon ElastiCache for distributed deployments.
  • To harden the architecture for production, you can use hardware security module (HSM)-backed EJBCA signing keys through AWS CloudHSM or an on-premises HSM. OCSP response stapling reduces validation latency, and Certificate Transparency logs provide a full audit trail of issued certificates.
  • For multi-tenant deployments, you can create per-tenant Certificate Authorities or per-tenant delegation authorities for cryptographic tenant isolation. Combined with per-tenant AWS accounts, this delivers strong isolation between tenants.
  • You can also complement PKI-based agent identity with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles. Use PKI for agent-to-agent authentication and IAM for AWS service authorization. The two systems work independently, providing defense in depth.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, remove the resources created during this walkthrough:

  • Delete the Amazon RDS for MySQL instance (or the AWS CloudFormation stack if you used the scripted setup).
  • Delete all secrets from AWS Secrets Manager, including user certificates and agent certificates under the 
    mcp/
    prefix.
  • Remove the verified sender email address from Amazon SES.
  • Terminate the Amazon EC2 instances running Keycloak and EJBCA (if deployed for this demonstration).
  • Revoke and delete all test certificates in EJBCA by using the EJBCA admin console or REST API.
  • Remove the Keycloak realm (
    mcp-realm
    ) and associated clients.
  • If you used the scripted setup, run 
    ./scripts/cleanup.sh
    (Linux) or 
    ./scripts/cleanup.bat
    (Windows) to automate these steps.

Conclusion

In this post, we demonstrated a reference architecture for securing AI agent communications using X.509 PKI with Keyfactor EJBCA and AWS services. The architecture addresses the fundamental identity gap in multi-agent AI systems through four complementary mechanisms:

  • Signed request envelopes provide cryptographic proof-of-possession on every inter-agent call, making it significantly harder for an unauthorized party to forge an agent’s identity or replay its requests.
  • User-signed delegation assertions decouple authorization from credential sharing. Agents prove they are authorized to act on the user’s behalf without holding the user’s private key or full-session token.
  • RFC 8693 audience-scoped tokens limit the scope of exposure from any token disclosure to a single service boundary.
  • Real-time OCSP revocation checking confirms that credential revocation takes immediate effect across the entire system. Revoking one user certificate promptly ends all downstream agent authority.

This architecture is framework-agnostic. While we demonstrated it with the AWS Strands Agents SDK and FastMCP, the same PKI patterns apply to LangChain, CrewAI, AutoGen, or any other multi-agent framework that uses tool protocols. As AI agents proliferate and gain access to increasingly sensitive operations, agent identity infrastructure moves from optional to essential.

To get started with this reference architecture, see the accompanying GitHub repository. For more information about the services used, see the following resources:
